title: Microsoft Azure Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate
realWorldValue: SC-500 earns the Microsoft Certified: Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate credential, validating the ability to design and implement end-to-end security controls across Azure, hybrid, and AI-enabled environments. It builds on the AZ-500 foundation and adds a dedicated AI security layer covering Copilot, Microsoft Entra Agent ID, and Azure AI Foundry guardrails — making it the go-to certification as organisations deploy AI workloads at scale. Assessed areas include identity and governance, network and storage security, compute hardening, and posture management with Defender for Cloud, Sentinel, and Microsoft Security Copilot.

skills: 1.1.1: Implement and configure Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
questions.question:
During a security audit, your organization identifies that several administrators hold permanent Global Administrator assignments in Microsoft Entra ID. You must reduce standing privilege while still allowing those administrators to perform tasks when needed, and require justification plus approval before privileges are activated.

What should you configure?

choices.text: Convert the assignments to PIM eligible role assignments and enable approval and justification in the role settings
choices.explanation: Eligible assignments require activation, and role settings enforce approval and justification on activation.

choices.text: Create a Conditional Access policy that blocks Global Administrator sign-ins unless a manager approves the session
choices.explanation: Conditional Access cannot capture per-activation approval for directory roles.

choices.text: Assign the administrators to a security group with a custom role that lacks Global Administrator permissions
choices.explanation: Removing the role entirely defeats the requirement to allow activation when needed.

choices.text: Enable access reviews on the Global Administrator role and require quarterly attestation
choices.explanation: Access reviews validate continued need but do not enforce per-activation approval or justification.

questions.tip: Focus on how PIM separates eligibility from activation.
questions.explanation:
Privileged Identity Management distinguishes eligible from active assignments to remove standing privilege while preserving the ability to elevate on demand.

**Why it works:** Eligible assignments require the user to activate the role, and role settings let you require approval and justification at activation time.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Conditional Access policy approval: Conditional Access governs sign-in conditions, not role activation approvals.
- Custom role replacement: Stripping Global Administrator removes the ability to perform required tasks.
- Access reviews only: Reviews confirm ongoing need but do not enforce just-in-time activation controls.

skills: 1.1.1: Implement and configure Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
questions.question:
The operations team wants to use Privileged Identity Management to control just-in-time elevation for the Contributor role on a specific Azure subscription. The assignments must be made through PIM rather than directly in Access control (IAM).

Which PIM feature should you use?

choices.text: PIM for Azure resources, scoped to the subscription, with eligible Contributor assignments
choices.explanation: PIM for Azure resources manages just-in-time activation of Azure RBAC roles at resource scopes.

choices.text: PIM for Microsoft Entra roles, assigning the Contributor role at the directory scope
choices.explanation: Microsoft Entra roles in PIM do not manage Azure RBAC role assignments on subscriptions.

choices.text: PIM for Groups, making the users eligible members of a group assigned the Owner role
choices.explanation: Owner exceeds the Contributor requirement and groups are not required when the role itself is supported in PIM.

choices.text: Azure Policy with a deny effect that blocks Contributor assignments outside PIM
choices.explanation: Azure Policy cannot enforce just-in-time activation of role assignments.

questions.tip: Distinguish between Microsoft Entra roles and Azure resource roles in PIM.
questions.explanation:
PIM has separate experiences for Microsoft Entra roles and Azure resource roles, and Contributor on a subscription is an Azure RBAC role.

**Why it works:** PIM for Azure resources supports eligible assignments at management group, subscription, resource group, and resource scopes, including the Contributor role.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Microsoft Entra roles option: Entra role PIM does not control Azure RBAC role assignments.
- PIM for Groups with Owner: Owner grants more rights than required and the role is directly supported.
- Azure Policy deny: Policy does not provide an activation workflow.

skills: 1.1.1: Implement and configure Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
questions.question:
Management has decided that privileged role assignments must be periodically validated. You need to ensure that eligible assignments to the User Administrator role are reviewed every 90 days and that any reviewer decision to deny continued access automatically removes the assignment.

Which TWO actions should you take?

choices.text: Create an access review in PIM for the User Administrator role with a recurrence of every 90 days
choices.explanation: PIM access reviews target privileged roles with configurable recurrence.

choices.text: Set the review's Upon completion settings to remove access for denied users automatically
choices.explanation: Auto-apply of denied results removes the assignment without manual intervention.

choices.text: Configure a Conditional Access policy that blocks the User Administrator role after 90 days
choices.explanation: Conditional Access cannot remove role assignments based on review outcomes.

choices.text: Enable continuous access evaluation on the tenant to revoke sessions after each review
choices.explanation: CAE revokes tokens on policy events, not based on access review denials.

choices.text: Create a Microsoft Entra entitlement management access package that expires after 90 days
choices.explanation: Entitlement management governs package assignments, not direct PIM role assignments.

questions.tip: Two settings combine: the schedule and what happens on denial.
questions.explanation:
PIM access reviews are designed exactly for this scenario and have automation for denied outcomes.

**Why it works:** Creating a recurring review establishes the cadence, and enabling automatic removal of denied users ensures denied decisions immediately remove the eligible assignment.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Conditional Access block: CA does not remove role assignments based on attestation.
- Continuous access evaluation: CAE handles session revocation events, not review outcomes.
- Entitlement management package: Access packages do not directly review existing PIM role assignments.

skills: 1.1.2: Implement conditional access policies
questions.question:
The security team must ensure that all users accessing Microsoft 365 from outside corporate networks complete multifactor authentication. Trusted IPs in the named locations list represent the corporate networks, and the policy must not affect access from those locations.

Which Conditional Access configuration should you use?

choices.text: Assign all users and cloud apps Office 365, exclude the trusted named location under Locations, and require multifactor authentication as a grant control
choices.explanation: Excluding the trusted location ensures the policy only applies outside the corporate network.

choices.text: Assign all users and cloud apps Office 365, include the trusted named location, and require multifactor authentication
choices.explanation: Including the trusted location would force MFA on internal users.

choices.text: Block access for all users when sign-in risk is high and exclude the trusted named location
choices.explanation: Risk-based block does not satisfy the requirement to MFA all external sign-ins.

choices.text: Require compliant device for Office 365 and exclude the trusted named location
choices.explanation: Device compliance is not the same control as MFA and does not meet the stated requirement.

questions.tip: Think about how location conditions and grant controls combine.
questions.explanation:
Conditional Access uses inclusions and exclusions to scope policies. Excluding the corporate network ensures MFA is only enforced externally.

**Why it works:** Targeting all users and Office 365, excluding the trusted location, and requiring MFA matches the requirement exactly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Including trusted location: That forces MFA on internal users, the opposite of intent.
- Risk-based block: Blocking on risk doesn't enforce MFA on every external sign-in.
- Compliant device: A different control that doesn't satisfy the MFA requirement.

skills: 1.1.2: Implement conditional access policies
questions.question:
Following a board decision to restrict data exfiltration, you must prevent users from downloading files from SharePoint Online when accessing from unmanaged devices, while still allowing browser-based viewing.

Which Conditional Access control should you configure?

choices.text: A session control that uses app-enforced restrictions for SharePoint Online to allow limited browser-only access on unmanaged devices
choices.explanation: App-enforced restrictions tell SharePoint to apply limited access for sessions flagged by Conditional Access.

choices.text: A grant control that requires the device to be marked as compliant in Intune
choices.explanation: That blocks unmanaged devices entirely instead of allowing view-only access.

choices.text: A grant control that requires the device to be Microsoft Entra hybrid joined
choices.explanation: Hybrid join requirements block unmanaged devices rather than enabling restricted access.

choices.text: A session control that sets sign-in frequency to 1 hour on unmanaged devices
choices.explanation: Sign-in frequency controls reauthentication cadence, not download restrictions.

questions.tip: The difference between blocking and restricting often lives in session controls.
questions.explanation:
Conditional Access session controls integrate with SharePoint Online's limited access feature via app-enforced restrictions.

**Why it works:** App-enforced restrictions instruct SharePoint to disable download, print, and sync while permitting browser view.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Require compliant device: Blocks unmanaged devices entirely.
- Hybrid join: Same blocking behavior, not restricted access.
- Sign-in frequency: Affects reauth, not download capability.

skills: 1.1.2: Implement conditional access policies
questions.question:
Arrange the steps to safely deploy a new Conditional Access policy that requires MFA for guest users accessing Azure management.

Place the steps in the correct order from first to last.

choices.text: Define the policy scope by selecting guest and external users as the target and Microsoft Azure Management as the cloud app
choices.explanation: Scoping users and apps is the first design step.

choices.text: Create the policy in report-only mode to evaluate impact without enforcement
choices.explanation: Report-only mode validates policy behavior using sign-in logs before enforcement.

choices.text: Review the Conditional Access workbook and sign-in logs to confirm expected matches and no unintended exclusions
choices.explanation: Validation precedes turning the policy on.

choices.text: Switch the policy to On to enforce MFA for matching sign-ins
choices.explanation: Enforcement happens only after validation.

questions.tip: Microsoft recommends validating impact before enforcing a new policy.
questions.explanation: Microsoft's deployment guidance follows scope, report-only, validate, then enforce to minimize lockout risk.

skills: 1.1.3: Implement and configure authentication methods, including multifactor authentication (MFA) and passwordless
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating phishing-resistant authentication methods for executives. They need a method that works on shared workstations without requiring user-owned hardware tokens, integrates with Microsoft Entra ID, and supports MFA in a single gesture.

Which authentication method should you deploy?

choices.text: Windows Hello for Business with cloud Kerberos trust on the shared workstations
choices.explanation: Windows Hello for Business provides phishing-resistant MFA via biometrics or PIN tied to the device TPM.

choices.text: SMS-based one-time codes as a secondary factor with passwords
choices.explanation: SMS is susceptible to phishing and SIM-swap attacks and is not phishing-resistant.

choices.text: Voice call verification as the secondary factor for sign-in
choices.explanation: Voice call MFA is phishable through social engineering and not recommended for high-value accounts.

choices.text: Email-based one-time passcodes routed to the user's mailbox
choices.explanation: Email OTPs are not phishing-resistant and depend on mailbox security.

questions.tip: Phishing resistance and single-gesture sign-in narrow the list to specific methods.
questions.explanation:
Windows Hello for Business satisfies phishing resistance and integrated MFA in one gesture.

**Why it works:** The credential is bound to device hardware and unlocked locally with biometrics or PIN, providing two factors phishing-resistantly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SMS codes: Vulnerable to phishing and SIM swap.
- Voice call: Phishable and weak factor.
- Email OTP: Inherits mailbox risks and is not phishing-resistant.

skills: 1.1.3: Implement and configure authentication methods, including multifactor authentication (MFA) and passwordless
questions.question:
You are migrating from the legacy MFA and self-service password reset method controls to the consolidated authentication methods policy in Microsoft Entra ID. You must enable FIDO2 security keys for the Finance group while keeping it disabled for other users.

What should you configure?

choices.text: In the Authentication methods policy, enable FIDO2 security key and target the Finance group as Include
choices.explanation: The authentication methods policy lets you enable a method and scope it to specific groups.

choices.text: Enable FIDO2 in the legacy per-user MFA settings page
choices.explanation: Legacy per-user MFA does not manage FIDO2 keys.

choices.text: Create a Conditional Access policy granting access only when FIDO2 is used by Finance
choices.explanation: CA can require methods at sign-in but cannot enable or register them.

choices.text: Enable security defaults and add Finance users to the Authenticator rollout
choices.explanation: Security defaults are tenant-wide and do not selectively enable FIDO2 keys.

questions.tip: Method enablement and method enforcement are different controls.
questions.explanation:
The authentication methods policy is the central place to enable and scope methods like FIDO2.

**Why it works:** Enabling FIDO2 in the policy and including only the Finance group restricts the method exactly as required.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Legacy MFA settings: Predates and does not manage FIDO2.
- Conditional Access: Enforces conditions at sign-in but does not enable methods.
- Security defaults: Tenant-wide and not selectable per group.

skills: 1.1.3: Implement and configure authentication methods, including multifactor authentication (MFA) and passwordless
questions.question: Match each Microsoft Entra authentication method to its primary characteristic.

slots.label: FIDO2 security key
Microsoft Authenticator passwordless phone sign-in
Temporary Access Pass
OATH hardware token

choices.text: Phishing-resistant hardware credential using WebAuthn standards
choices.explanation: FIDO2 keys provide phishing-resistant MFA via WebAuthn.

choices.text: Approval-based mobile sign-in that replaces the password with a number-match prompt
choices.explanation: Authenticator passwordless phone sign-in approves sign-ins without a password.

choices.text: Time-limited passcode used to bootstrap registration of stronger methods
choices.explanation: TAP issues a short-lived code to onboard or recover passwordless users.

choices.text: Time-based one-time password generated by a physical device
choices.explanation: OATH hardware tokens generate TOTP codes on a small hardware device.

questions.tip: Identify which method is hardware versus app-based and which is for onboarding.
questions.explanation: Each method has a distinct role: FIDO2 for phishing-resistant MFA, Authenticator for app-based passwordless, TAP for onboarding, and OATH tokens for hardware TOTP.

skills: 1.1.4: Implement and configure identity for applications, including enterprise applications and app registrations
questions.question:
The organization is looking to deploy a new internal web application that signs in users with Microsoft Entra ID. Developers must be able to define API permissions and configure redirect URIs, while a separate operations team controls which users can access the deployed app.

Which combination should you use?

choices.text: Create an app registration for developers to define the application object, and use the corresponding enterprise application (service principal) for assignment and sign-in control
choices.explanation: App registration owns the application object while the enterprise app exposes assignment and SSO settings.

choices.text: Create only an enterprise application and add API permissions directly under its Properties blade
choices.explanation: API permissions and redirect URIs are managed on the application object via app registration.

choices.text: Create only an app registration and assign users to it directly from the Owners blade
choices.explanation: User assignment for sign-in is performed on the enterprise application, not on the app registration.

choices.text: Create a managed identity in the subscription and assign the developers the Application Administrator role
choices.explanation: Managed identities are for Azure resources, not for user-facing web apps.

questions.tip: Application object and service principal are two sides of the same identity.
questions.explanation:
Microsoft Entra represents apps with a global application object and a per-tenant service principal.

**Why it works:** Developers configure the app via the registration and operations governs user assignment and SSO via the enterprise application.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Enterprise app only: Cannot define API permissions or redirect URIs there.
- App registration only: User assignment lives on the service principal.
- Managed identity: Designed for Azure workloads, not user-facing apps.

skills: 1.1.4: Implement and configure identity for applications, including enterprise applications and app registrations
questions.question:
You manage an enterprise application that federates with a SaaS service. Only users in the Sales group should be able to sign in, and any other user attempting access must be denied without becoming a member.

What should you configure on the enterprise application?

choices.text: Set 'Assignment required?' to Yes and assign the Sales group to the application
choices.explanation: Enabling assignment required restricts sign-in to assigned users and groups.

choices.text: Add the Sales group as an owner of the enterprise application
choices.explanation: Owners manage the app object but ownership does not gate sign-in.

choices.text: Create a Conditional Access policy that requires the Sales group, leaving Assignment required set to No
choices.explanation: Without assignment required, non-Sales users could still sign in if the CA policy doesn't apply universally.

choices.text: Restrict the SAML reply URL to a Sales-only subdomain
choices.explanation: Reply URL restrictions affect token destinations, not which users can sign in.

questions.tip: User assignment is enforced by a specific app setting.
questions.explanation:
Enterprise applications have an explicit toggle to require assignment before sign-in.

**Why it works:** With assignment required on, only users or groups explicitly assigned can sign in to the app.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Group as owner: Owners manage configuration, not sign-in scope.
- CA without assignment required: Other users could still sign in based on policy gaps.
- Reply URL restriction: Controls token return, not who can authenticate.

skills: 1.1.4: Implement and configure identity for applications, including enterprise applications and app registrations
questions.question:
To reduce credential theft risk, you must remove client secrets from a confidential client app registration that calls Microsoft Graph and replace them with a stronger credential type. The application runs on a server you control.

Which TWO actions should you take?

choices.text: Upload a certificate to the app registration's Certificates and secrets blade
choices.explanation: Certificate credentials replace shared secrets with key-based authentication.

choices.text: Update the application code to authenticate using the certificate private key when acquiring tokens
choices.explanation: The client must present the certificate to obtain access tokens.

choices.text: Enable public client flows on the app registration
choices.explanation: Public client flows are for native or single-page apps and weaken security here.

choices.text: Configure the redirect URI to localhost to use device code flow
choices.explanation: Device code flow targets input-constrained scenarios, not server-side calls.

choices.text: Grant the app the User.Read delegated permission to Microsoft Graph
choices.explanation: Permission scope does not address credential type.

questions.tip: Both the credential store and the client code must change together.
questions.explanation:
Moving from client secrets to certificates requires uploading the credential and changing the auth flow in code.

**Why it works:** Uploading the certificate registers the public key with Microsoft Entra, and the client uses the private key to assert its identity during token acquisition.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Public client flows: Designed for non-confidential clients.
- Device code flow: Not appropriate for a server backend.
- Graph delegated scope: Permission grant unrelated to credential type.

skills: 1.1.5: Manage OAuth permission grants and consent settings
questions.question:
During a security audit, the team finds that users have consented to several third-party applications with broad Microsoft Graph permissions. You must stop new user consent to applications unless they meet a verified publisher and low-risk permissions threshold, while preserving productivity for trusted apps.

Which setting should you configure in Microsoft Entra ID?

choices.text: Set user consent to 'Allow user consent for apps from verified publishers, for selected permissions' under Consent and permissions
choices.explanation: This restricts user consent to verified publisher apps for a defined low-risk permission set.

choices.text: Set user consent to 'Allow user consent for apps' and rely on admin review of sign-in logs
choices.explanation: This keeps unrestricted consent and only audits after the fact.

choices.text: Disable enterprise applications tenant-wide and require Conditional Access for each new app
choices.explanation: Disabling apps blocks legitimate access and isn't a consent control.

choices.text: Set user consent to 'Do not allow user consent' and create a Conditional Access policy targeting Microsoft Graph
choices.explanation: Blocking all user consent removes productivity for trusted apps; the requirement allows selected scenarios.

questions.tip: Look for the consent option that combines verified publisher and a permission classification.
questions.explanation:
Microsoft Entra offers a graduated user consent option tied to verified publishers and admin-classified permissions.

**Why it works:** Limiting consent to verified publishers and classified low-risk permissions blocks risky grants while enabling trusted apps.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Allow all and audit: Doesn't prevent risky consent.
- Disable apps: Overly broad and unrelated to consent settings.
- Block all consent with CA: Removes productivity for trusted apps.

skills: 1.1.5: Manage OAuth permission grants and consent settings
questions.question:
The operations team wants end users to be able to request admin consent for applications that require permissions users cannot grant themselves. Reviewers must be notified and able to approve or deny requests from the portal.

What should you enable?

choices.text: The admin consent request workflow under Enterprise applications, designating reviewers and notification settings
choices.explanation: The admin consent workflow lets users request consent and routes requests to designated reviewers.

choices.text: Self-service group management so users can create groups that grant app permissions
choices.explanation: Group management does not handle OAuth permission consent.

choices.text: An access package in entitlement management that includes the application
choices.explanation: Access packages assign users to apps but do not collect consent requests.

choices.text: A Conditional Access policy that prompts for admin approval at sign-in
choices.explanation: Conditional Access does not provide an admin consent workflow.

questions.tip: Look for the built-in workflow tied to consent prompts.
questions.explanation:
Microsoft Entra's admin consent request feature converts blocked consent prompts into reviewable requests.

**Why it works:** Enabling the workflow lets users submit requests directly from the consent prompt and routes them to designated reviewers.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Self-service groups: Unrelated to OAuth consent.
- Access package: Assigns access but doesn't collect consent.
- Conditional Access: No consent workflow control.

skills: 1.1.5: Manage OAuth permission grants and consent settings
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending and risk reports, you discover an enterprise application has been granted the `Mail.ReadWrite` delegated permission across the tenant. You must revoke this permission grant for all users without deleting the application.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DelegatedPermissionGrant.ReadWrite.All"
$grants = Get-MgOauth2PermissionGrant -Filter "clientId eq 'abc...' and scope eq 'Mail.ReadWrite'"
```

Which cmdlet should you run next?

choices.text: `Remove-MgOauth2PermissionGrant -OAuth2PermissionGrantId $grants.Id`
choices.explanation: Removing the OAuth2PermissionGrant revokes the delegated permission for that client.

choices.text: `Remove-MgServicePrincipal -ServicePrincipalId $grants.ClientId`
choices.explanation: Removing the service principal deletes the application, which the requirement forbids.

choices.text: `Update-MgApplication -ApplicationId $grants.ClientId -RequiredResourceAccess @()`
choices.explanation: This edits the app registration's requested permissions, not granted permissions.

choices.text: `Disable-MgServicePrincipalSignIn -ServicePrincipalId $grants.ClientId`
choices.explanation: Disabling sign-in blocks the app entirely instead of removing the specific grant.

questions.tip: Distinguish between requested permissions, granted permissions, and the service principal itself.
questions.explanation:
OAuth2 permission grants are the records that bind a service principal to delegated scopes for users.

**Why it works:** Removing the OAuth2PermissionGrant entry removes only the delegated permission while preserving the app.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Remove-MgServicePrincipal: Deletes the application entirely.
- Update-MgApplication: Modifies requested permissions in the manifest, not granted consents.
- Disable sign-in: Blocks the app rather than removing the grant.

skills: 1.1.6: Implement and configure managed identities for Azure resources
questions.question:
Your team runs an Azure App Service that retrieves a connection string from Azure Key Vault. The application currently uses a service principal with a client secret stored in the app's configuration. You must remove the secret without storing credentials in code or configuration.

What should you configure?

choices.text: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the App Service and grant it the Key Vault Secrets User role on the key vault
choices.explanation: A system-assigned managed identity removes stored credentials and gets authorized via Azure RBAC on the vault.

choices.text: Store the client secret in Key Vault and reference it via a Key Vault reference in App Service configuration
choices.explanation: This still relies on a stored secret to authenticate to Key Vault initially.

choices.text: Create an app registration with a certificate credential and embed the certificate in the App Service image
choices.explanation: Embedding a certificate is still a credential in the deployment artifact.

choices.text: Enable Azure AD authentication on the App Service and add the service principal to the authorized users
choices.explanation: App Service authentication protects user sign-ins, not service-to-Key-Vault calls.

questions.tip: The point is to eliminate stored credentials entirely.
questions.explanation:
Managed identities provide an identity to the Azure resource without any credential in code or config.

**Why it works:** App Service obtains tokens from the IMDS endpoint using its system-assigned identity, and RBAC on the vault authorizes access.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Key Vault reference for secret: Still requires a secret somewhere.
- Cert in image: Embedded credentials are exactly what must be removed.
- App Service AAD auth: Governs user logins to the app, not outbound auth.

skills: 1.1.6: Implement and configure managed identities for Azure resources
questions.question:
The operations team needs a single identity that several Azure virtual machines in different subscriptions can share to access a common Azure Storage account. The identity must persist independently of the lifecycle of any individual VM.

Which identity type should you use?

choices.text: A user-assigned managed identity assigned to each VM and granted Storage Blob Data Reader on the storage account
choices.explanation: User-assigned identities are standalone resources that multiple Azure resources can share.

choices.text: A system-assigned managed identity enabled on one VM and shared with the others
choices.explanation: System-assigned identities are tied to a single resource and cannot be shared.

choices.text: A service principal with a client secret distributed to each VM via custom script extension
choices.explanation: This reintroduces stored credentials and is not a managed identity pattern.

choices.text: A workload identity federation between the VMs and a GitHub Actions OIDC issuer
choices.explanation: Workload identity federation is for external workloads, not VMs that can use managed identities natively.

questions.tip: Identify which managed identity type can be shared across resources.
questions.explanation:
User-assigned managed identities are first-class Azure resources you can attach to many compute instances.

**Why it works:** The identity persists independently and can be attached to VMs across subscriptions while RBAC permissions remain on the storage account.

**Why the others don't work:**
- System-assigned: One-to-one with a resource.
- Service principal with secret: Stored credentials defeat the purpose.
- Workload identity federation: Designed for external workloads.

skills: 1.1.6: Implement and configure managed identities for Azure resources
questions.question:
You are troubleshooting an Azure VM application that uses a system-assigned managed identity to call Azure Resource Manager. The application receives an HTTP 400 when requesting a token from the instance metadata service.

```bash
curl "http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?resource=https://management.azure.com/" \
  -H "Metadata:true"
```

What should you do to fix the request?

choices.text: Add the `api-version` query parameter, for example `api-version=2018-02-01`
choices.explanation: The IMDS token endpoint requires an api-version query parameter.

choices.text: Replace the IMDS endpoint with `https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/token`
choices.explanation: Managed identities use the IMDS endpoint, not the public AAD token endpoint.

choices.text: Add an Authorization header containing the VM's system-assigned identity client secret
choices.explanation: Managed identities have no client secret to add.

choices.text: Send the request as POST with a form-encoded body containing grant_type=client_credentials
choices.explanation: The IMDS token endpoint accepts GET with query parameters, not the client_credentials grant.

questions.tip: Check the required IMDS query parameters.
questions.explanation:
The Azure Instance Metadata Service token endpoint expects specific query parameters including api-version.

**Why it works:** Supplying api-version satisfies the IMDS contract and lets it issue a token for the requested resource.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AAD token endpoint: Managed identities use IMDS, not the AAD token endpoint directly.
- Authorization header with secret: There is no secret for a managed identity.
- POST with client_credentials: IMDS does not use the OAuth client_credentials grant.

skills: 1.2.1: Deploy Key Vault
questions.question:
The compliance team at a financial services firm requires that any deleted secret in a new Azure Key Vault cannot be permanently removed by an administrator for at least 90 days, even if the vault itself is deleted.

Which setting should you enable when deploying the vault?

choices.text: Enable purge protection with a 90 day retention period
choices.explanation: Purge protection blocks the purge operation during the retention window, preventing both administrators and Microsoft from forcibly removing soft-deleted objects.

choices.text: Enable soft-delete only with a 90 day retention period
choices.explanation: Soft-delete alone allows an administrator with Purge permission to immediately remove the deleted object before the retention period expires.

choices.text: Apply a resource lock of type CanNotDelete to the vault
choices.explanation: A delete lock prevents vault deletion but does not stop a privileged user from purging individual soft-deleted secrets within the vault.

choices.text: Configure a deny assignment on the Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/purge action
choices.explanation: Deny assignments are reserved for Azure managed scenarios such as Blueprints and cannot be authored directly by customers to block purge operations.

questions.tip: Consider which control specifically blocks the purge operation during the retention window.
questions.explanation:
Purge protection is the only Key Vault feature that mandates the full retention period must elapse before any soft-deleted object can be permanently removed.

**Why it works:** Once purge protection is enabled, the purge API is rejected for the duration of the retention period, regardless of caller permissions.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Soft-delete only: still allows an authorized caller to purge.
- Resource lock: protects the vault resource, not individual secret purges.
- Deny assignment: customers cannot author deny assignments directly.

skills: 1.2.1: Deploy Key Vault
questions.question:
You are deploying a new Azure Key Vault for a development team and want the vault to use Azure role-based access control for data plane operations from the moment it is created.

```bash
az keyvault create \
  --name dev-kv-eu-01 \
  --resource-group rg-dev-eu \
  --location westeurope
```

Which parameter should you add to the command?

choices.text: Add `--enable-rbac-authorization true` to the create command
choices.explanation: This flag sets the vault's permission model to Azure RBAC at creation, so all data plane access is governed by role assignments rather than access policies.

choices.text: Add `--default-action Deny` to the create command
choices.explanation: This parameter configures the network firewall default action and has no bearing on the data plane authorization model.

choices.text: Add `--enabled-for-deployment true` to the create command
choices.explanation: This permits Azure Resource Manager to retrieve secrets during VM deployment but does not change the permission model.

choices.text: Add `--bypass AzureServices` to the create command
choices.explanation: Bypass controls firewall exceptions for trusted Microsoft services and is unrelated to RBAC versus access policy selection.

questions.tip: Look for the flag that switches the permission model itself.
questions.explanation:
Setting `--enable-rbac-authorization true` at creation time configures the vault to use Azure RBAC for data plane authorization from the start.

**Why it works:** The permission model property is set during vault provisioning, eliminating the need to migrate from access policies later.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `--default-action Deny`: configures firewall behaviour, not authorization model.
- `--enabled-for-deployment`: governs ARM template integration only.
- `--bypass AzureServices`: a firewall exemption flag.

skills: 1.2.1: Deploy Key Vault
questions.question:
The platform team is deploying a new production Azure Key Vault that will store HSM-backed keys and must be protected against accidental or malicious deletion.

Arrange the following deployment steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Choose the subscription, resource group, vault name, and region
choices.explanation: Basic resource identity must be established before any vault-specific options can be configured.

choices.text: Select the Premium pricing tier to enable HSM-backed keys
choices.explanation: Tier selection determines available key types and must be set before recovery and access settings.

choices.text: Enable soft-delete and purge protection with a retention period
choices.explanation: Recovery options are configured during creation; purge protection cannot be disabled once enabled.

choices.text: Set the permission model to Azure role-based access control
choices.explanation: Choosing the authorization model determines how subsequent role assignments or access policies are applied.

choices.text: Review and create the vault, then assign Key Vault Administrator at the resource scope
choices.explanation: Final review provisions the vault, after which RBAC role assignments can be made to grant data plane access.

questions.tip: Recovery features must be locked in before final provisioning, and roles can only be assigned after the resource exists.
questions.explanation: Vault identity is chosen first, then tier, then recovery settings, then the permission model, and finally the resource is created before any role assignments. Purge protection is a deploy-time decision, so it must be selected before the resource is committed.

skills: 1.2.2: Configure Key Vault settings
questions.question:
During a security audit, the audit team requests that every secret read on the production Azure Key Vault be retained in a queryable store for 12 months.

What should you configure?

choices.text: Create a diagnostic setting on the vault that streams the AuditEvent log to a Log Analytics workspace with a 12 month retention
choices.explanation: Diagnostic settings forward Key Vault data plane events including secret reads to Log Analytics where retention can be set to 12 months.

choices.text: Enable the Activity Log export to a storage account with a 365 day immutability policy
choices.explanation: The Activity Log captures management plane operations only and does not record data plane events like individual secret reads.

choices.text: Turn on Microsoft Defender for Key Vault and increase the alert retention to 12 months
choices.explanation: Defender for Key Vault generates security alerts but is not a general-purpose audit log for every secret access.

choices.text: Enable Microsoft Entra sign-in logs and filter by the Key Vault application identifier
choices.explanation: Entra sign-in logs capture authentication events, not the specific Key Vault data plane operation that occurred.

questions.tip: Audit trails for data plane operations require a specific telemetry pipeline.
questions.explanation:
A diagnostic setting that sends the AuditEvent category to Log Analytics captures all data plane operations including individual secret reads.

**Why it works:** Key Vault emits an AuditEvent for each get, list, set, and delete on a secret, key, or certificate, and Log Analytics retention can be configured to 12 months.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Activity Log: management plane only.
- Defender for Key Vault: alerts, not a full audit log.
- Entra sign-in logs: authentication, not authorized operation detail.

skills: 1.2.2: Configure Key Vault settings
questions.question:
The platform team enabled soft-delete on a production Azure Key Vault six months ago but did not enable purge protection. A new compliance policy now requires that purge protection be active.

What should you do?

choices.text: Update the vault and set `enablePurgeProtection` to true, accepting that the property cannot be disabled afterwards
choices.explanation: Purge protection can be enabled on an existing vault that already has soft-delete on, but once set the flag is irreversible.

choices.text: Delete and redeploy the vault with both soft-delete and purge protection enabled from the start
choices.explanation: Redeployment is unnecessary because purge protection can be turned on in-place when soft-delete is already enabled.

choices.text: Apply an Azure Policy that audits vaults without purge protection and rely on the audit effect alone
choices.explanation: Audit policies report non-compliance but do not change the vault configuration to meet the requirement.

choices.text: Place a CanNotDelete lock on the vault to substitute for purge protection
choices.explanation: A resource lock blocks deletion of the vault but does not block purging of individual soft-deleted secrets, keys, or certificates.

questions.tip: Some Key Vault toggles are deploy-time-or-later one-way switches.
questions.explanation:
Purge protection can be turned on after the fact provided soft-delete is already enabled, but the change is permanent.

**Why it works:** Setting `enablePurgeProtection` to true on the existing vault meets the compliance requirement without redeployment.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Redeploy: unnecessary disruption.
- Audit policy: visibility only.
- CanNotDelete lock: does not prevent purge of soft-deleted objects.

skills: 1.2.2: Configure Key Vault settings
questions.question: Match each Azure Key Vault setting to the behaviour it controls.

slots.label: `enableSoftDelete`
`enablePurgeProtection`
`enabledForTemplateDeployment`
`enableRbacAuthorization`

choices.text: Retains deleted secrets and keys in a recoverable state for the configured retention period
choices.explanation: Soft-delete preserves deleted objects so they can be restored within the retention window.

choices.text: Blocks the purge operation during the retention window even for privileged callers
choices.explanation: Purge protection enforces that the full retention period elapses before permanent deletion.

choices.text: Allows Azure Resource Manager to retrieve secrets when an ARM template references the vault
choices.explanation: This flag permits ARM template deployments to pull secrets from the vault at deployment time.

choices.text: Switches the data plane authorization model from access policies to Azure role assignments
choices.explanation: Enabling this property makes the vault use Azure RBAC for keys, secrets, and certificates.

questions.tip: Distinguish recovery features from access integration features.
questions.explanation: Each toggle controls a distinct vault behaviour: recovery, irreversibility of purge, template integration, and authorization model.

skills: 1.2.3: Configure access to Key Vault
questions.question:
The operations team needs an application's managed identity to read and list secrets from a production Azure Key Vault that uses the Azure role-based access control permission model. The identity must not be able to create, update, or delete any vault content.

Which role should you assign?

choices.text: Assign the Key Vault Secrets User role at the vault scope
choices.explanation: This built-in role grants read and list permissions on secret contents without any write or management privileges.

choices.text: Assign the Key Vault Secrets Officer role at the vault scope
choices.explanation: Secrets Officer permits create, update, and delete on secrets, exceeding the read-only requirement.

choices.text: Assign the Key Vault Reader role at the vault scope
choices.explanation: Key Vault Reader allows viewing vault metadata and secret properties but not the secret values themselves.

choices.text: Assign the Reader role at the resource group scope
choices.explanation: The classic Reader role grants management plane visibility only and provides no data plane access to secrets.

questions.tip: Match the role to data plane read of secret contents only.
questions.explanation:
Key Vault Secrets User is the least-privilege role that grants only read and list of secret values.

**Why it works:** The role is purpose-built for applications that need to retrieve secrets without managing them.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Secrets Officer: write access included.
- Key Vault Reader: cannot read secret values.
- Reader: management plane only.

skills: 1.2.3: Configure access to Key Vault
questions.question:
Following a board decision to standardize on Azure RBAC, the security team plans to migrate a legacy Azure Key Vault from the vault access policy model to the Azure role-based access control model. The vault currently has 30 access policies in place.

What should you do first?

choices.text: Inventory the existing access policies and assign equivalent Key Vault data plane roles before switching the permission model
choices.explanation: Switching the model immediately invalidates all existing access policies, so equivalent role assignments must be planned and made before the cutover.

choices.text: Switch the permission model to Azure RBAC and then create role assignments based on which applications report errors
choices.explanation: Cutting over first causes an outage because all data plane access stops working until role assignments are in place.

choices.text: Delete the vault and redeploy it with the RBAC permission model selected at creation
choices.explanation: Redeployment is destructive and unnecessary; the permission model can be changed on the existing vault.

choices.text: Assign Owner at the subscription scope to each application identity to guarantee continuity during migration
choices.explanation: Granting Owner widely violates least privilege and provides excessive permissions far beyond Key Vault data plane needs.

questions.tip: Plan the new authorization state before flipping the switch.
questions.explanation:
Mapping each access policy to an equivalent Key Vault data plane role assignment before changing the permission model prevents an outage.

**Why it works:** Once the model is switched, only RBAC role assignments are evaluated, so they must already be in place.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cutover first: causes loss of access.
- Redeploy: destructive and unnecessary.
- Owner assignment: massive over-privilege.

skills: 1.2.3: Configure access to Key Vault
questions.question: Match each Azure Key Vault built-in role to the access it grants.

slots.label: Key Vault Administrator
Key Vault Certificates Officer
Key Vault Crypto User
Key Vault Reader

choices.text: Full management of keys, secrets, and certificates including purge
choices.explanation: Administrator covers all data plane operations across every object type.

choices.text: Create, import, update, and delete certificates within the vault
choices.explanation: Certificates Officer manages certificate lifecycle without granting key or secret write access.

choices.text: Perform cryptographic operations such as sign, verify, wrap, and unwrap using existing keys
choices.explanation: Crypto User exercises keys for cryptographic work but cannot create or delete them.

choices.text: View vault metadata and object properties without access to secret values or key material
choices.explanation: Reader is metadata-only and excludes any secret value or key material disclosure.

questions.tip: Distinguish lifecycle management roles from use-only roles.
questions.explanation: Key Vault data plane roles separate full administration, per-object-type lifecycle management, cryptographic use, and read-only metadata visibility.

skills: 1.2.4: Configure firewall settings on Key Vault
questions.question:
The security team needs to ensure that only a specific virtual network subnet hosting application workloads can reach a production Azure Key Vault, while blocking all other public network traffic.

Which firewall configuration should you apply?

choices.text: Set the default action to Deny and add the application subnet as a virtual network rule on the vault
choices.explanation: A Deny default combined with a virtual network service endpoint rule restricts access to the named subnet only.

choices.text: Set the default action to Allow and add the application subnet IP range as an IP rule
choices.explanation: An Allow default leaves the vault open to all public traffic regardless of any additional allow rules.

choices.text: Enable Trusted Microsoft Services bypass and add the subnet CIDR as an IP rule
choices.explanation: Trusted services bypass only affects Microsoft platform services and does not restrict third-party public traffic when the default remains Allow.

choices.text: Disable public network access entirely and add the subnet as an IP rule
choices.explanation: Disabling public access blocks all public endpoint traffic including from the application subnet unless private endpoints are used.

questions.tip: Restriction requires both a deny default and a specific allow rule.
questions.explanation:
Setting Deny as the default and explicitly allowing the application subnet via a virtual network rule produces a precise allow-list.

**Why it works:** Key Vault evaluates virtual network rules only when the default is Deny, and the service endpoint binds the subnet identity to the rule.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Allow default: leaves the vault open.
- Bypass with Allow default: still open.
- Disable public access: requires private endpoints to function.

skills: 1.2.4: Configure firewall settings on Key Vault
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating how to make an Azure Key Vault reachable only from on-premises servers connected via ExpressRoute, with no traffic traversing the Azure public endpoint at all.

What should you configure?

choices.text: Create a private endpoint for the vault in a connected virtual network and disable public network access on the vault
choices.explanation: Private endpoints expose the vault via a private IP that on-premises clients can reach over ExpressRoute, while disabling public access removes the public endpoint entirely.

choices.text: Add the on-premises public IP ranges to the vault firewall and set the default action to Deny
choices.explanation: This still routes traffic over the public endpoint, which the requirement explicitly prohibits.

choices.text: Enable service endpoints for Microsoft.KeyVault on the gateway subnet and set Deny by default
choices.explanation: Service endpoints work for Azure-hosted clients in the subnet, not for on-premises hosts.

choices.text: Configure the vault to bypass Trusted Microsoft Services for ExpressRoute gateway traffic
choices.explanation: Trusted services bypass is for Azure platform services, not for ExpressRoute customer traffic.

questions.tip: Eliminating the public endpoint requires a private IP path.
questions.explanation:
A private endpoint plus disabled public access ensures on-premises clients reach the vault only over private connectivity.

**Why it works:** ExpressRoute private peering can route to the private endpoint IP, and public network access being off removes the public endpoint as an attack surface.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Public IP firewall: still uses the public endpoint.
- Service endpoint on gateway subnet: not applicable to on-premises traffic.
- Trusted services bypass: not applicable to customer traffic.

skills: 1.2.4: Configure firewall settings on Key Vault
questions.question:
The organization is looking to lock down an Azure Key Vault so that only an Azure Functions app and the Azure Backup service can reach it from outside a private virtual network.

Which TWO actions should you take?

choices.text: Set the firewall default action to Deny on the vault
choices.explanation: A Deny default establishes the implicit block needed before exceptions take effect.

choices.text: Enable the Allow trusted Microsoft services bypass on the vault
choices.explanation: Azure Backup is in the trusted services list and gains access through the bypass, while the Function App reaches the vault via its outbound IPs or VNet integration.

choices.text: Set the firewall default action to Allow and add ranges for trusted services
choices.explanation: Allow leaves the vault open to all public traffic, defeating the lockdown goal.

choices.text: Disable soft-delete on the vault to streamline firewall evaluation
choices.explanation: Soft-delete is unrelated to firewall behaviour and disabling it weakens recovery posture.

choices.text: Add 0.0.0.0/0 to the IP allow list to ensure Microsoft services connect
choices.explanation: Allowing the whole internet eliminates the firewall's purpose.

questions.tip: Lockdown needs an explicit deny baseline plus a controlled exception.
questions.explanation:
Together these two settings create a deny-by-default vault that still permits the trusted Microsoft services list.

**Why it works:** The Deny default blocks unsolicited public access, and the trusted services bypass admits Azure Backup; the Function App reaches the vault through its own configured network path.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Allow default: removes the lockdown.
- Disable soft-delete: unrelated and harmful.
- 0.0.0.0/0: opens the vault to everyone.

skills: 1.2.5: Manage keys, secrets, and certificates
questions.question:
The application team stores a database connection string as a secret in Azure Key Vault and wants client applications to always pick up the latest value without code changes or redeployments.

Which approach should you implement?

choices.text: Have applications reference the secret without a version identifier so the latest enabled version is returned
choices.explanation: Omitting the version segment in the secret URI causes Key Vault to return the current version automatically when the secret is rotated.

choices.text: Update each application's configuration with the new version identifier whenever the secret rotates
choices.explanation: This requires a code or configuration change on every rotation, defeating the no-redeployment requirement.

choices.text: Replace the secret with a certificate and embed the connection string in the certificate's tags
choices.explanation: Tags are metadata not intended for sensitive runtime data, and certificates are not a substitute for secret values.

choices.text: Store the connection string in an environment variable on the application host and copy from the vault nightly
choices.explanation: This loses the live-rotation property and reintroduces stale credentials between syncs.

questions.tip: Look at how Key Vault URIs differ when a version is omitted.
questions.explanation:
Referencing a secret by its name URI without a version returns whichever version is currently the latest enabled one.

**Why it works:** Key Vault treats the unversioned URI as a pointer to the current secret, so rotation flows through transparently to callers.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Update per version: defeats the requirement.
- Tags: not designed for sensitive data.
- Nightly copy: stale between rotations.

skills: 1.2.5: Manage keys, secrets, and certificates
questions.question:
Management has decided that all TLS certificates used by Azure App Service apps should be renewed automatically by Azure Key Vault using a public certificate authority that is integrated with the vault.

What should you configure on each certificate?

choices.text: A certificate issuance policy that names an integrated issuer such as DigiCert or GlobalSign and sets a lifetime action to auto-renew before expiry
choices.explanation: Issuance policies define the issuer and lifetime actions that trigger automatic renewal with an integrated public CA.

choices.text: A secret rotation policy that issues a new self-signed certificate every 60 days
choices.explanation: Secret rotation policies apply to secrets and self-signed certificates do not satisfy the public CA requirement.

choices.text: An Event Grid subscription on the vault that triggers a Logic App to request a renewed certificate
choices.explanation: While possible, this bypasses the built-in integrated issuer mechanism that natively supports auto-renewal.

choices.text: A managed HSM key rotation policy with a notify-before-expiry action
choices.explanation: Key rotation policies apply to keys in Managed HSM, not to certificates issued from a public CA.

questions.tip: Native auto-renewal is driven by the certificate's own policy.
questions.explanation:
Configuring an issuance policy with an integrated issuer and a lifetime action enables Key Vault to renew the certificate automatically.

**Why it works:** Key Vault has built-in integration with several public CAs and can submit renewal requests on schedule when the policy specifies them.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Self-signed rotation: fails the public CA requirement.
- Event Grid + Logic App: works but ignores the built-in feature.
- HSM key rotation: different object type entirely.

skills: 1.2.5: Manage keys, secrets, and certificates
questions.question:
The cryptography team is configuring automatic key rotation on an RSA encryption key stored in Azure Key Vault.

Arrange the following steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Assign Key Vault Crypto Officer to the identity that will manage rotation settings
choices.explanation: Permissions to author rotation policy must exist before the policy can be set.

choices.text: Define a rotation policy on the key specifying the rotation interval and notify-before-expiry action
choices.explanation: The policy declares when and how the key should rotate automatically.

choices.text: Set the expiration time on the current key version so the policy's lifetime actions have a reference point
choices.explanation: Lifetime actions are evaluated relative to the expiration time of each version.

choices.text: Wait for the policy to create a new version or trigger an on-demand rotation to validate the configuration
choices.explanation: Validation confirms the rotation policy produces a new version as designed.

choices.text: Update dependent applications to reference the key by unversioned URI so they consume the rotated version
choices.explanation: Without an unversioned reference, applications remain pinned to the previous version after rotation.

questions.tip: Permissions and configuration must precede validation, and downstream references come last.
questions.explanation: Permissions, policy definition, expiration setting, validation, and consumer URI update form the correct order to enable end-to-end automatic rotation.

skills: 1.2.6: Scan for secrets by using Defender Cloud Security Posture Management (Defender CSPM)
questions.question:
The security team wants Microsoft Defender for Cloud to discover plaintext credentials such as connection strings and SSH keys stored on Azure virtual machines, without requiring agents to be installed on each VM.

Which plan should you enable?

choices.text: Enable the Defender CSPM plan at the subscription scope to activate agentless secret scanning for VMs
choices.explanation: Agentless secret scanning of VMs is a feature included in the paid Defender CSPM plan.

choices.text: Enable the Foundational CSPM free plan and turn on the secret scanning extension
choices.explanation: Foundational CSPM is free but does not include agentless secret scanning, which requires the paid Defender CSPM plan.

choices.text: Enable Defender for Servers Plan 1 and install the Log Analytics agent on each VM
choices.explanation: Defender for Servers focuses on threat protection for compute and does not provide the agentless secret discovery surface.

choices.text: Enable Defender for Key Vault to scan VM disks for secrets that reference vault URIs
choices.explanation: Defender for Key Vault detects suspicious data plane activity on vaults and does not scan VM disks for plaintext secrets.

questions.tip: Agentless secret scanning is a paid CSPM capability.
questions.explanation:
Defender CSPM is the paid plan that activates agentless secret scanning of VMs.

**Why it works:** Defender CSPM snapshots VM disks and inspects them for plaintext secrets such as cloud credentials and SSH keys without requiring agents.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Foundational CSPM: free tier excludes this feature.
- Defender for Servers: different protection focus.
- Defender for Key Vault: protects the vault itself, not VMs.

skills: 1.2.6: Scan for secrets by using Defender Cloud Security Posture Management (Defender CSPM)
questions.question:
Following enablement of Defender CSPM, the security operations team wants to prioritize remediation by viewing the secrets that are exposed on internet-facing VMs and that grant access to highly privileged cloud resources.

Where should they look?

choices.text: Use Cloud Security Explorer in Defender for Cloud with a query that correlates exposed VMs to discovered secrets and target resource permissions
choices.explanation: Cloud Security Explorer is the graph-based query tool that joins attack path entities such as VM exposure and secret targets to highlight high-impact findings.

choices.text: Use the Azure Resource Graph Explorer to query Microsoft.KeyVault resources for recent access events
choices.explanation: Resource Graph does not surface Defender CSPM secret findings or correlate them with VM exposure and target privilege.

choices.text: Open the Microsoft Sentinel incidents pane and filter by the Defender for Key Vault alert source
choices.explanation: Defender for Key Vault alerts cover vault data plane anomalies, not VM-resident plaintext secrets discovered by CSPM.

choices.text: Open Microsoft Entra Identity Protection and review risky service principals associated with the discovered secrets
choices.explanation: Identity Protection assesses sign-in risk for identities and does not correlate secret discovery with VM exposure.

questions.tip: Cross-entity prioritization needs a graph view.
questions.explanation:
Cloud Security Explorer's attack-path-aware queries join exposed compute with discovered secrets and their permissions for prioritized remediation.

**Why it works:** Defender CSPM populates a security graph that the explorer queries to surface chained risk.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Resource Graph: lacks the security context.
- Sentinel Defender for Key Vault: wrong data source.
- Identity Protection: different risk dimension.

skills: 1.2.6: Scan for secrets by using Defender Cloud Security Posture Management (Defender CSPM)
questions.question:
To reduce the risk of credential theft from Azure VMs, management has approved deployment of Defender CSPM across all production subscriptions.

Which TWO actions should you take to begin agentless secret scanning of VMs?

choices.text: Enable the Defender CSPM plan in Microsoft Defender for Cloud at the subscription scope
choices.explanation: Enabling the paid CSPM plan is the prerequisite that turns on the suite of agentless extensions including secret scanning.

choices.text: Turn on the Agentless scanning for machines extension within the Defender CSPM plan settings
choices.explanation: Secret scanning relies on the agentless machine scanning component, which must be enabled in the plan extensions.

choices.text: Install the Azure Monitor Agent on every VM that contains sensitive workloads
choices.explanation: Agentless scanning explicitly does not require agents on VMs, so installing AMA is unnecessary for this feature.

choices.text: Create a Microsoft Sentinel workspace and onboard each VM via the Sentinel agent
choices.explanation: Sentinel onboarding is for SIEM scenarios and is not required for Defender CSPM secret discovery.

choices.text: Enable Defender for Key Vault on every subscription to allow CSPM to access vault metadata
choices.explanation: Defender for Key Vault is a separate plan focused on vault threats and is not a prerequisite for VM secret scanning.

questions.tip: The capability lives inside a specific plan and depends on a specific extension.
questions.explanation:
Enabling the Defender CSPM plan and turning on agentless machine scanning together activate VM secret discovery.

**Why it works:** The plan provides licensing and the extension drives the disk snapshot inspection that finds plaintext secrets.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AMA install: not required for agentless scanning.
- Sentinel onboarding: unrelated.
- Defender for Key Vault: separate plan and scope.

skills: 1.2.7: Implement Defender for Key Vault
questions.question:
The security team wants Microsoft Defender for Cloud to generate alerts when an anomalous principal accesses an Azure Key Vault from an unfamiliar location.

What should you enable?

choices.text: Enable Microsoft Defender for Key Vault on the subscription containing the vaults
choices.explanation: This plan provides behavioural analytics over vault data plane access and generates the unfamiliar location alerts described.

choices.text: Enable Defender CSPM on the subscription and onboard the vault as a monitored resource
choices.explanation: Defender CSPM focuses on posture and secret discovery, not real-time data plane anomaly detection on vaults.

choices.text: Turn on diagnostic logging for the vault and create a Log Analytics alert for non-default geographies
choices.explanation: Custom log queries can approximate this, but they do not replicate the trained anomaly detection delivered by Defender for Key Vault.

choices.text: Enable Microsoft Entra Conditional Access named locations and apply them to Key Vault sign-ins
choices.explanation: Conditional Access governs identity authentication, not Key Vault data plane access anomaly detection.

questions.tip: Threat detection on a specific Azure service comes from its dedicated Defender plan.
questions.explanation:
Microsoft Defender for Key Vault is the plan that delivers behavioural alerts on suspicious vault access patterns.

**Why it works:** The plan analyses telemetry from Key Vault data plane operations and raises alerts for anomalies such as unfamiliar IPs or principals.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Defender CSPM: posture-oriented, not anomaly alerts on vault access.
- Custom log queries: lack the trained detection model.
- Conditional Access locations: control sign-in, not data plane.

skills: 1.2.7: Implement Defender for Key Vault
questions.question:
During a security audit, Defender for Cloud raises an alert that a previously unseen IP address has performed a high volume of secret retrievals from a production Azure Key Vault. The on-call engineer needs to contain the incident immediately.

What should you do first?

choices.text: Identify the source IP from the alert and update the vault firewall to deny access from that address while validating the activity
choices.explanation: The first containment step is to block the unfamiliar IP at the vault firewall so further unauthorized retrievals stop while investigation continues.

choices.text: Delete the affected secrets and recreate them with new values before notifying any stakeholders
choices.explanation: Rotation is part of remediation, but it should follow containment so the attacker cannot capture the new values during the same session.

choices.text: Disable Defender for Key Vault temporarily to suppress further alerts during triage
choices.explanation: Disabling the detection plan removes visibility precisely when it is most needed.

choices.text: Reduce the vault's soft-delete retention period to immediately purge any compromised secrets
choices.explanation: Soft-delete retention cannot be reduced once enabled and purging does not stop active unauthorized access.

questions.tip: Contain the network path before rotating data.
questions.explanation:
Blocking the suspect IP at the vault firewall halts the unauthorized access channel so the team can investigate and then rotate secrets safely.

**Why it works:** The Defender alert provides the source IP, which can be added to a deny posture on the vault firewall to immediately stop the activity.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Rotate first: leaves the access path open during rotation.
- Disable Defender: removes detection visibility.
- Reduce soft-delete: not possible and does not contain the threat.

skills: 1.2.7: Implement Defender for Key Vault
questions.question:
After Defender for Key Vault raises a high-severity alert for suspicious data plane activity on a production vault, the incident response team begins their playbook.

Arrange the following response steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Identify the source IP address and caller identity from the alert details
choices.explanation: Triage starts by extracting the actor and origin so subsequent actions are targeted.

choices.text: Enable or tighten the vault firewall to block the offending source IP
choices.explanation: Network-level containment stops further unauthorized data plane calls.

choices.text: Restrict the vault's access policy or RBAC assignment to remove the compromised principal's permissions
choices.explanation: Identity-level containment ensures the attacker cannot return through another network path with the same credentials.

choices.text: Rotate the secrets, keys, and certificates that were accessed during the incident window
choices.explanation: Any material the attacker may have exfiltrated must be replaced so it can no longer be used.

choices.text: Review audit logs and update detection rules to capture similar future patterns
choices.explanation: Post-incident lessons feed back into monitoring to harden against repeat attacks.

questions.tip: Investigate, then contain by network, then by identity, then rotate, then learn.
questions.explanation: The recommended Defender for Key Vault response sequence is identify the source IP, enable the firewall, restrict the access policy, rotate affected secrets, and review for continuous improvement.

skills: 1.3.1: Implement and configure security controls by using Azure Policy, including built-in and custom policy definitions
questions.question:
During a security review, the cloud governance team finds that developers continue to create storage accounts that allow public blob access. The team needs to block any new storage account creation that does not have public access disabled, with no possibility of override at deployment time.

Which Azure Policy effect should they configure on the policy definition?

choices.text: Deny
choices.explanation: Deny rejects non-compliant resource create or update requests at the ARM evaluation stage.

choices.text: Audit, which records non-compliant resource creations in the activity log for review by the governance team
choices.explanation: Audit only logs non-compliance and does not block the request, so the storage account would still be created.

choices.text: DeployIfNotExists, which provisions a remediation action whenever a non-compliant storage account is detected
choices.explanation: DeployIfNotExists triggers a remediation deployment after resource creation but does not block the original non-compliant resource.

choices.text: Modify, which appends the required property to the resource at deployment to make it compliant
choices.explanation: Modify alters request properties such as tags or specific aliases, but it is not used to refuse creation based on blob public access settings.

questions.tip: Identify which effect intercepts the request before the resource is created.
questions.explanation:
Deny is the only effect that blocks creation of non-compliant resources during the request evaluation phase.

**Why it works:** When a create or update request is evaluated, Deny returns a failure if the resource does not meet the policy rule, so the storage account is never provisioned.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Audit: only logs non-compliance, the resource is still created.
- DeployIfNotExists: triggers post-creation remediation, not blocking.
- Modify: changes specific properties such as tags, not used to prevent blob public access.

skills: 1.3.1: Implement and configure security controls by using Azure Policy, including built-in and custom policy definitions
questions.question:
The platform team needs to apply 18 related Azure Policy definitions to every subscription in a management group. They want a single assignment object with shared parameters and one compliance view per scope.

Which Azure Policy construct should they use?

choices.text: Create an initiative (policy set) definition that includes the 18 policies and assign it at the management group
choices.explanation: Initiatives group related policies into a single assignment with unified parameters and consolidated compliance reporting.

choices.text: Assign each of the 18 policy definitions individually to every subscription in the management group
choices.explanation: Individual assignments produce 18 separate compliance views per subscription and require duplicating parameters.

choices.text: Combine the 18 policies into a single policy definition with multiple `if` blocks in the policy rule
choices.explanation: A policy definition supports one rule and one effect, so 18 distinct policies cannot be merged into one definition.

choices.text: Create a Resource Manager template that deploys the 18 policy assignments and run it at each subscription
choices.explanation: Templated assignments still produce 18 separate assignment objects without unified compliance reporting.

questions.tip: Look for a construct that groups multiple definitions under one assignment.
questions.explanation:
An initiative (policy set) is the supported way to bundle multiple definitions into one assignable object.

**Why it works:** Initiatives roll up 18 individual definitions into a single assignment scope with shared parameters and one compliance view in Azure Policy.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Individual assignments: produce fragmented compliance reporting.
- Merged policy rule: a definition has a single rule and effect.
- ARM template of assignments: still creates 18 distinct assignments.

skills: 1.3.1: Implement and configure security controls by using Azure Policy, including built-in and custom policy definitions
questions.question:
The security team wants Azure Policy to automatically deploy the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint extension on any Windows virtual machine that is missing it. They plan to use a DeployIfNotExists policy assigned at a subscription scope.

Which TWO configurations must be in place for remediation to succeed against existing resources?

choices.text: Assign a managed identity to the policy assignment with the role definitions specified in the policy's `roleDefinitionIds`
choices.explanation: DeployIfNotExists assignments require a managed identity granted the listed roles to perform the remediation deployment.

choices.text: Create a remediation task that targets existing non-compliant VMs in the subscription
choices.explanation: A remediation task is required to apply DeployIfNotExists to resources that already existed before the assignment.

choices.text: Set the policy effect to Deny so that only compliant VMs can exist
choices.explanation: Deny blocks creation but does not deploy the extension to existing or new VMs.

choices.text: Enable diagnostic settings on every VM and stream logs to Log Analytics
choices.explanation: Diagnostic settings are unrelated to the remediation mechanism for DINE policies.

choices.text: Grant the policy assignment a service principal in the subscription's Microsoft Entra tenant
choices.explanation: Policy assignments use a managed identity, not a separately created service principal.

questions.tip: Consider both the identity that performs remediation and the action that applies it to existing resources.
questions.explanation:
DeployIfNotExists relies on a managed identity for deployment and a remediation task to act on pre-existing non-compliant resources.

**Why it works:** The managed identity holds the roles needed to deploy the extension, and the remediation task triggers the deployment against existing VMs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Deny: blocks creation, never deploys extensions.
- Diagnostic settings: unrelated to policy remediation.
- Manual service principal: policy uses its own managed identity.

skills: 1.3.2: Evaluate regulatory compliance by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.question:
The compliance officer asks which regulatory standard is automatically applied to every Azure subscription enrolled in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, even before any other standards are added.

Which standard is enabled by default?

choices.text: Microsoft cloud security benchmark
choices.explanation: MCSB is the default standard assigned to every subscription onboarded to Defender for Cloud.

choices.text: PCI DSS v4.0
choices.explanation: PCI DSS is available to add manually but is not enabled by default.

choices.text: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5
choices.explanation: NIST 800-53 is an optional standard the customer must add to the compliance dashboard.
ISO 27001 is available to add but is not assigned automatically on onboarding.

questions.tip: Recall which baseline Microsoft applies to every Defender for Cloud subscription out of the box.
questions.explanation:
Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) is the default regulatory and security baseline in Defender for Cloud.

**Why it works:** MCSB is automatically assigned to every subscription enrolled in Defender for Cloud and underpins the default Secure Score and compliance view.

**Why the others don't work:**
- PCI DSS v4.0: optional, must be added manually.
- NIST 800-53: optional, must be added manually.
- ISO 27001: optional, must be added manually.

skills: 1.3.2: Evaluate regulatory compliance by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.question:
The bank's auditors require evidence that the organization tracks compliance against NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 across all production subscriptions. Microsoft Defender for Cloud is already enabled with the default standard.

What should the security team do to make NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 visible in the regulatory compliance dashboard?
