choices.text: Add the NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 standard to the subscriptions from the Security policies page in Defender for Cloud
choices.explanation: Additional regulatory standards are assigned from the Security policies blade and then appear in the compliance dashboard.

choices.text: Create a custom Azure Policy initiative that mirrors NIST SP 800-53 controls and assign it at the tenant root
choices.explanation: Defender for Cloud ships a built-in NIST initiative; building a custom one duplicates work and is not how the dashboard surfaces standards.

choices.text: Upgrade every subscription to the Defender CSPM plan and wait for NIST to appear automatically
choices.explanation: Defender CSPM does not auto-apply NIST 800-53; the standard must be explicitly added.

choices.text: Export the Microsoft cloud security benchmark mapping to NIST and treat MCSB compliance as the auditor evidence
choices.explanation: Although MCSB maps to NIST, auditors require the NIST standard itself enabled to produce the compliance report.

questions.tip: Think about how additional standards are surfaced in the compliance dashboard.
questions.explanation:
Regulatory standards beyond MCSB are added through the Security policies blade for each subscription.

**Why it works:** Adding NIST 800-53 Rev. 5 from Security policies registers the standard against the subscription and produces a dedicated compliance view in the dashboard.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Custom initiative: duplicates a built-in standard and does not register in the regulatory dashboard the same way.
- Defender CSPM upgrade: does not auto-add NIST.
- MCSB mapping: helpful context but not the same as enabling the NIST standard.

skills: 1.3.2: Evaluate regulatory compliance by using Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.question:
Following a board decision, the organization must report compliance against an internal control framework that is not represented by any built-in standard in Microsoft Defender for Cloud.

Which TWO actions are required to surface compliance against the internal framework in the Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance dashboard?

choices.text: Create a custom security standard in Defender for Cloud that represents the internal framework
choices.explanation: Custom standards are how non-built-in frameworks are modelled in the compliance dashboard.

choices.text: Add the relevant built-in and custom recommendations to the custom standard so they map to its controls
choices.explanation: A standard is meaningful only when populated with recommendations whose results drive the compliance score.

choices.text: Export the Microsoft cloud security benchmark to CSV and edit the rows in place
choices.explanation: Editing MCSB is not supported and would not represent the internal framework as a separate standard.

choices.text: Open a Microsoft support ticket to have the internal framework added to the built-in catalogue
choices.explanation: Microsoft does not add private organizational frameworks to the built-in catalogue.

choices.text: Enable continuous export of Secure Score to Log Analytics and build a custom workbook
choices.explanation: A workbook visualization does not register a standard against the regulatory compliance dashboard.

questions.tip: Consider both the container and the controls that populate it.
questions.explanation:
Custom regulatory tracking requires creating a custom standard and populating it with recommendations.

**Why it works:** The custom standard becomes a first-class entry in the regulatory dashboard, and the attached recommendations drive its compliance score.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Editing MCSB: not supported and not framework-specific.
- Support ticket: Microsoft does not curate private frameworks.
- Workbook export: dashboards do not replace standards.

skills: 1.3.3: Implement and configure security controls in Defender for Cloud, including security standards and recommendations
questions.question:
The security team reviews the Defender for Cloud Recommendations page and sees a recommendation flagged as Quick Fix eligible. They want to remediate it across all affected resources without writing custom automation.

What should they do?

choices.text: Select the recommendation, choose the affected resources, and use the built-in Fix action to apply the remediation
choices.explanation: Quick Fix in Defender for Cloud applies the prescribed remediation to selected resources directly from the portal.

choices.text: Export the recommendation to a CSV file and open a service request asking Microsoft Support to apply the fix
choices.explanation: Microsoft Support does not remediate customer recommendations on the tenant's behalf.

choices.text: Create a Logic App that subscribes to the recommendation and runs an ARM template to remediate each resource
choices.explanation: Logic Apps automation is possible but is not the simplest built-in option when the recommendation is Quick Fix eligible.

choices.text: Disable the recommendation in the active policy so that it no longer appears in Secure Score
choices.explanation: Disabling hides the recommendation but does not remediate the underlying risk.

questions.tip: Look for the built-in remediation control on a Quick Fix eligible recommendation.
questions.explanation:
Quick Fix eligible recommendations expose a Fix button that applies the remediation directly.

**Why it works:** The Fix action invokes the prescribed change against the selected resources with no custom code required.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Support request: Microsoft does not remediate customer resources.
- Custom Logic App: unnecessary when Quick Fix exists.
- Disabling: removes visibility, not the risk.

skills: 1.3.3: Implement and configure security controls in Defender for Cloud, including security standards and recommendations
questions.question:
Management has decided to prioritise improvements that produce the largest Secure Score uplift. The team is unsure which unit Secure Score uses when ranking improvement potential in Microsoft Defender for Cloud.

What is the unit of measurement that drives Secure Score?

choices.text: Security controls, where each control groups related recommendations and contributes a maximum point value to the score
choices.explanation: Secure Score is calculated per security control, and each control awards its maximum points only when all its recommendations are healthy for a resource.

choices.text: Individual recommendations, each contributing one point regardless of severity or grouping
choices.explanation: Recommendations contribute through their parent control, not as flat per-recommendation points.

choices.text: Regulatory standards, where each enabled standard adds a fixed score component
choices.explanation: Regulatory standards influence compliance views but are not the Secure Score scoring unit.

choices.text: Defender plans, with one point granted per enabled plan per subscription
choices.explanation: Enabling Defender plans surfaces more recommendations but does not award score points directly.

questions.tip: Consider how Defender for Cloud groups recommendations when calculating impact.
questions.explanation:
Secure Score is built around security controls that group recommendations and grant points when all recommendations in the control are healthy.

**Why it works:** Each control has a maximum value; partial credit is given proportionally to the healthy resources in that control.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Per-recommendation points: not how the scoring model works.
- Regulatory standards: drive compliance, not Secure Score units.
- Defender plans: gate features, not score points.

skills: 1.3.3: Implement and configure security controls in Defender for Cloud, including security standards and recommendations
questions.question: Match each Microsoft Defender for Cloud capability to the security outcome it primarily provides.

slots.label: Defender CSPM attack path analysis
Microsoft cloud security benchmark
Workload protection plan for servers
Custom recommendation

choices.text: Default baseline of security controls assigned to every onboarded subscription
choices.explanation: Maps to the Microsoft cloud security benchmark which is enabled by default.

choices.text: Visualization of chained risks that an attacker could exploit across cloud resources
choices.explanation: Attack path analysis is a Defender CSPM capability.

choices.text: Runtime threat detection on virtual machines with alerts on suspicious processes
choices.explanation: Defender for Servers provides workload threat detection.

choices.text: Organization-defined check authored as an Azure Policy and added to a standard
choices.explanation: Custom recommendations are authored via custom policy definitions.

questions.tip: Distinguish posture baseline from posture risk visualization, workload threat detection, and customization.
questions.explanation: Each Defender for Cloud capability serves a distinct purpose: posture baseline, posture risk visualization, workload threat detection, or customization.

skills: 1.3.4: Implement resource locks
questions.question:
The finance director asks the platform team to prevent accidental deletion of a production SQL database while still allowing schema and data updates by the application team.

Which resource lock level should the team apply to the SQL database?

choices.text: CanNotDelete on the SQL database resource
choices.explanation: CanNotDelete blocks delete requests while still allowing reads and updates to the resource.

choices.text: ReadOnly on the SQL database resource
choices.explanation: ReadOnly would prevent the application team from making any modifications, including schema or data changes performed through the control plane.

choices.text: Deny assignment on the resource group containing the database
choices.explanation: Deny assignments come from Azure Blueprints or managed apps and are not the standard mechanism for accidental deletion protection.

choices.text: Azure Policy with the Deny effect on `Microsoft.Sql/servers/databases`
choices.explanation: Azure Policy can block new deployments but is not the recommended way to prevent deletion of an existing resource.

questions.tip: Match the lock level to the exact operation that must be blocked.
questions.explanation:
CanNotDelete blocks deletion while permitting all other control-plane updates.

**Why it works:** The lock denies DELETE operations against the resource but allows the application team to continue performing PATCH and PUT operations.

**Why the others don't work:**
- ReadOnly: blocks updates as well.
- Deny assignment: comes from Blueprints/managed apps.
- Policy with Deny: targets new deployments, not the protect-from-deletion case.

skills: 1.3.4: Implement resource locks
questions.question:
The security team places a CanNotDelete lock on a storage account that holds critical blob backups. A developer later reports that they can still delete individual blobs from the container.

Why is blob deletion still possible?

choices.text: Resource locks apply only to control-plane operations on the resource, not to data-plane operations such as blob delete
choices.explanation: Locks affect Azure Resource Manager operations; blob delete is a data-plane action handled by the storage service.

choices.text: CanNotDelete is inherited by child resources, but blob containers are not considered child resources of the storage account
choices.explanation: Inheritance is not the issue; locks simply do not cover data-plane requests at all.

choices.text: The developer has the Owner role, which always bypasses any lock placed on a resource
choices.explanation: Locks apply regardless of role; even Owner cannot delete a locked resource without removing the lock.

choices.text: Soft delete on the storage account converts deletion to a recoverable state that the lock cannot reach
choices.explanation: Soft delete is independent of resource locks and is not why blob deletion succeeds.

questions.tip: Distinguish between control-plane and data-plane operations.
questions.explanation:
Resource locks target ARM (control-plane) requests; they do not gate data-plane API calls.

**Why it works:** Blob delete calls hit the storage service's REST endpoint directly, which is not evaluated against the resource lock.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Inheritance: locks do inherit, but data-plane is the relevant distinction.
- Owner bypass: locks apply to all roles.
- Soft delete: a recovery feature, unrelated to locks.

skills: 1.3.4: Implement resource locks
questions.question:
The operations team needs to enforce resource locks across the production landing zone. They want any lock placed on a parent scope to apply to every child resource automatically and to ensure that only specific principals can remove locks.

Which TWO statements are correct about Azure resource locks?

choices.text: Locks placed at a parent scope, such as a resource group, are inherited by all child resources within that scope
choices.explanation: Locks cascade from subscriptions and resource groups down to the resources they contain.

choices.text: Adding or removing locks requires the `Microsoft.Authorization/locks/*` permission, typically granted via Owner or User Access Administrator
choices.explanation: Lock management is gated by the locks RBAC action, present in Owner and User Access Administrator.

choices.text: Locks override role assignments, so a user without the relevant data action can still delete locked resources
choices.explanation: Locks restrict actions further; they do not override RBAC to grant additional permissions.

choices.text: Contributor role includes the permissions required to create and remove resource locks by default
choices.explanation: Contributor explicitly excludes `Microsoft.Authorization/*` actions, including lock management.

choices.text: ReadOnly locks allow PATCH operations against tags but block POST operations on the resource
choices.explanation: ReadOnly blocks all write operations on the resource, including tag updates and POST.

questions.tip: Think about inheritance and the specific permission needed to manage locks.
questions.explanation:
Locks inherit downward, and modifying them requires the locks RBAC action that is part of Owner or User Access Administrator.

**Why it works:** Inheritance ensures one lock can protect many resources; restricting `Microsoft.Authorization/locks/*` keeps lock management privileged.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Locks overriding RBAC: locks only restrict, never grant.
- Contributor managing locks: Contributor lacks the authorization actions.
- ReadOnly allowing tag PATCH: ReadOnly blocks writes including tag updates.

skills: 1.3.5: Manage Azure built-in role assignments
questions.question:
The operations lead must grant a new SRE the ability to manage all resources in a subscription, including creating role assignments for others, but without authority to change the subscription's billing relationship.

Which built-in role should be assigned at the subscription scope?

choices.text: Owner
choices.explanation: Owner grants full management of resources, including delegating access through role assignments, without changing billing.

choices.text: Contributor
choices.explanation: Contributor can manage resources but cannot grant access to others because it excludes the `Microsoft.Authorization/*` actions.

choices.text: User Access Administrator
choices.explanation: User Access Administrator can manage access but cannot manage resources themselves.

choices.text: Reader
choices.explanation: Reader provides only view access and cannot create or manage resources.

questions.tip: Identify the role that combines full resource management with access delegation.
questions.explanation:
Owner is the built-in role that combines full resource control with the ability to manage role assignments.

**Why it works:** Owner includes `*` actions plus the authorization data actions needed to assign other principals.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Contributor: lacks authorization actions.
- User Access Administrator: lacks resource management.
- Reader: read-only.

skills: 1.3.5: Manage Azure built-in role assignments
questions.question:
You are configuring access for a vendor team that needs Contributor permissions on three specific resource groups, but no access to anything else in the subscription.

At which scope should the role assignment be created?

choices.text: Create three separate Contributor role assignments, one at each of the resource group scopes
choices.explanation: Scoping each assignment to the resource group grants the required access without leaking permissions to the rest of the subscription.

choices.text: Create one Contributor assignment at the subscription scope and use deny assignments to exclude other resource groups
choices.explanation: Deny assignments cannot be authored by customers outside of Blueprints or managed apps, so this is not a supported pattern.

choices.text: Create one Contributor assignment at the management group containing the subscription
choices.explanation: Management group scope is broader than the subscription and grants far more access than required.

choices.text: Assign Reader at the subscription and Contributor at each individual resource
choices.explanation: Reader at the subscription leaks unnecessary access and Contributor at each resource is overly granular.

questions.tip: Pick the smallest scope that contains exactly the required resources.
questions.explanation:
Resource group scope is the smallest container that matches the requirement of access to exactly those three groups.

**Why it works:** Three discrete assignments at the resource group scope grant Contributor only where needed.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Deny assignments: not customer-authored.
- Management group scope: too broad.
- Reader plus per-resource Contributor: leaks Reader and is overly granular.

skills: 1.3.5: Manage Azure built-in role assignments
questions.question: Match each task to the most appropriate Azure built-in role.

slots.label: Manage only role assignments without managing resources
Read and write key material in an Azure Key Vault using RBAC permissions model
View Azure resources without making changes
Manage all resources in a subscription without delegating access

choices.text: Reader
choices.explanation: Read-only access to view resources.

choices.text: User Access Administrator
choices.explanation: Dedicated to managing access without managing resources.

choices.text: Key Vault Crypto Officer
choices.explanation: Granular Key Vault data-plane role for managing key material.

choices.text: Contributor
choices.explanation: Full resource management excluding access delegation.

questions.tip: Distinguish access-management roles from resource-management roles and data-plane roles.
questions.explanation: Each role aligns to a specific axis: read-only viewing, access delegation, Key Vault data-plane management, or resource management.

skills: 1.3.6: Manage custom roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
questions.question:
The platform team is creating a custom Azure role that grants restart permissions on virtual machines across two specific subscriptions. They want to author the role once and assign it at both subscriptions, but no broader.

Which value should they include in the `assignableScopes` array of the role definition?

choices.text: The resource IDs of both subscriptions, listed individually in `assignableScopes`
choices.explanation: Custom Azure roles support multiple subscription scopes listed explicitly in `assignableScopes`.

choices.text: The tenant root `/` to allow assignment anywhere in the organization
choices.explanation: Custom Azure roles cannot use `/` as an assignable scope; only management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, or resources are allowed.

choices.text: The resource group IDs of every VM the role should manage
choices.explanation: Listing every resource group adds maintenance and exceeds the requirement to scope at subscription level.

choices.text: A wildcard `*` to match any subscription created in the future
choices.explanation: Wildcards are not supported in `assignableScopes` for custom Azure roles.

questions.tip: Recall what values `assignableScopes` accepts for a custom Azure role.
questions.explanation:
Custom Azure roles allow multiple subscription IDs in `assignableScopes` so the role can be assigned at exactly those scopes.

**Why it works:** ARM evaluates the role's assignable scopes when an assignment is created; both subscriptions are valid targets.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Tenant root `/`: not allowed for Azure roles.
- Per-resource-group: unnecessary granularity.
- Wildcards: unsupported.

skills: 1.3.6: Manage custom roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
questions.question:
The identity team needs to delegate management of a specific Microsoft Entra application's credentials to a helpdesk group without granting broad directory privileges.

Which approach should they use?

choices.text: Create a custom Microsoft Entra role that includes the credential management permissions and scope it to that application
choices.explanation: Entra custom roles can be scoped to a single application registration, enabling fine-grained delegation.

choices.text: Assign the Application Administrator role at directory scope to the helpdesk group
choices.explanation: Application Administrator grants tenant-wide application management, exceeding what is required.

choices.text: Create a custom Azure RBAC role with the application permissions and assign it at the subscription scope
choices.explanation: Application registration permissions are part of the Entra resource provider, not Azure RBAC.

choices.text: Add the helpdesk group as an owner of every application object in the tenant
choices.explanation: Tenant-wide ownership grants more access than needed for a single application.

questions.tip: Match the requirement for fine-grained directory delegation to the appropriate role system.
questions.explanation:
Microsoft Entra custom roles support per-application scope, which is the supported way to delegate management of a single app registration.

**Why it works:** A custom Entra role assigned at the application scope grants only the listed credential management actions.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Application Administrator: tenant-wide, too broad.
- Custom Azure role: Azure RBAC does not control Entra app registrations.
- App owners on every app: also too broad.

skills: 1.3.6: Manage custom roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
questions.question: Match each custom role characteristic to the role system that supports it.

slots.label: Defined with `actions`, `notActions`, `dataActions`, `notDataActions`
Defined with `rolePermissions` referencing `allowedResourceActions` on directory objects
Assignable at management group, subscription, resource group, or resource scope
Assignable at tenant scope or on a single application registration

choices.text: Custom Azure role
choices.explanation: Azure RBAC custom roles target ARM resources and use the actions/notActions schema.

choices.text: Custom Microsoft Entra role
choices.explanation: Entra custom roles target directory objects and use the rolePermissions schema.

questions.tip: Distinguish ARM-targeted roles from directory-targeted roles.
questions.explanation: Azure custom roles govern ARM resources with action-based permissions; Entra custom roles govern directory objects with resource-action-based permissions.

skills: 1.3.7: Evaluate and remediate overprivileged access assignments by using Azure role-based access control (RBAC)
questions.question:
During a quarterly access review, the security team needs to identify principals in Azure that hold permissions they have not used in the last 90 days, then right-size their assignments.

Which service should they use to surface this insight?

choices.text: Microsoft Entra Permissions Management
choices.explanation: Permissions Management calculates a Permissions Creep Index by comparing granted permissions against permissions actually used.

choices.text: Microsoft Defender for Identity
choices.explanation: Defender for Identity detects identity threats on-premises but does not analyze unused Azure RBAC permissions.

choices.text: Microsoft Sentinel UEBA
choices.explanation: UEBA detects anomalous behaviour but is not designed to baseline permission usage versus assignments.

choices.text: Azure Policy compliance dashboard
choices.explanation: Azure Policy reports compliance against rules, not unused permissions per identity.

questions.tip: Look for the CIEM tool in the Microsoft Entra family.
questions.explanation:
Microsoft Entra Permissions Management is the CIEM service that highlights unused permissions for right-sizing.

**Why it works:** It compares granted versus used permissions and produces remediation guidance via the Permissions Creep Index.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Defender for Identity: on-premises identity threat detection.
- Sentinel UEBA: behaviour analytics, not entitlement management.
- Azure Policy: rule compliance, not usage.

skills: 1.3.7: Evaluate and remediate overprivileged access assignments by using Azure role-based access control (RBAC)
questions.question:
The audit team reports that several engineers hold permanent Owner assignments on production subscriptions. The CISO wants to retain their ability to act when needed while removing standing access.

What should the security team configure?

choices.text: Convert the Owner assignments to eligible assignments in Privileged Identity Management with approval and MFA on activation
choices.explanation: PIM eligible assignments remove standing access while preserving just-in-time elevation with controls.

choices.text: Replace the Owner assignments with Contributor and grant Owner only to a break-glass account
choices.explanation: Contributor removes the ability to manage role assignments, which the engineers may legitimately need on activation.

choices.text: Remove the Owner assignments entirely and rely on Azure Lighthouse delegations from a partner tenant
choices.explanation: Azure Lighthouse is for cross-tenant management and is not the standard pattern for internal JIT elevation.

choices.text: Move the engineers into a security group and lower the group assignment to Reader
choices.explanation: Reader does not allow the engineers to perform their owner-level tasks even when required.

questions.tip: Look for a mechanism that supports just-in-time activation rather than permanent removal.
questions.explanation:
Privileged Identity Management eligible assignments deliver JIT activation with approval and MFA, removing standing access while keeping operational capability.

**Why it works:** Engineers activate Owner only when needed; activation can be gated by approval, MFA, and time bounds.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Contributor swap: removes legitimate authorization actions.
- Lighthouse: cross-tenant scenario.
- Reader: too restrictive even on activation.

skills: 1.3.7: Evaluate and remediate overprivileged access assignments by using Azure role-based access control (RBAC)
questions.question:
The security team is running a remediation cycle for overprivileged Azure RBAC assignments using Microsoft Entra Permissions Management.

Arrange the following steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Onboard the Azure subscriptions to Microsoft Entra Permissions Management so usage data can be collected
choices.explanation: Collection of activity data is a prerequisite to any analysis.

choices.text: Review the Permissions Creep Index to identify identities with the largest gap between granted and used permissions
choices.explanation: The index ranks identities so the team focuses on the highest-impact accounts.

choices.text: Generate right-sized role recommendations and create the corresponding custom Azure roles or scoped built-in role assignments
choices.explanation: The remediation step replaces overprivileged assignments with appropriately scoped ones.

choices.text: Monitor the identities after remediation to confirm activity continues with reduced permissions
choices.explanation: Post-change monitoring validates that the right-sized permissions are sufficient.

questions.tip: Think in terms of collect, analyse, remediate, then verify.
questions.explanation: Permissions remediation follows a standard CIEM lifecycle: collect activity data, analyse over-permissioning, remediate, then verify.

skills: 1.3.8: Configure security controls for backup protection by using Azure Backup security features
questions.question:
Following a ransomware tabletop exercise, the operations team needs to ensure that if an attacker deletes a recovery point in a Recovery Services vault, the data can still be recovered for at least 14 days.

Which Azure Backup feature provides this protection?

choices.text: Soft delete for backup items in the Recovery Services vault
choices.explanation: Soft delete retains deleted backup data for a recoverable period by default before permanent removal.

choices.text: Cross-region restore from the paired Azure region
choices.explanation: Cross-region restore aids regional outages but does not protect against deletion of recovery points.

choices.text: Geo-redundant storage on the vault
choices.explanation: GRS replicates data but does not prevent loss when the recovery point itself is deleted.

choices.text: Backup reports through Azure Monitor
choices.explanation: Reports surface activity but do not retain deleted backup content.

questions.tip: Identify the feature designed to recover from deletion of backup items.
questions.explanation:
Soft delete protects backups from accidental or malicious deletion for a configurable retention period.

**Why it works:** When a backup item is deleted, Azure Backup retains it in a soft-deleted state and can be restored before purge.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cross-region restore: targets regional outages.
- GRS: storage replication, not deletion recovery.
- Reports: visibility only.

skills: 1.3.8: Configure security controls for backup protection by using Azure Backup security features
questions.question:
The CISO requires that destructive operations on a Recovery Services vault, such as disabling soft delete or reducing retention, require approval from a separate security tenant before the change can take effect.

Which Azure Backup capability should be enabled?

choices.text: Multi-user authorization (MUA) using a Resource Guard located in the security tenant
choices.explanation: MUA with a Resource Guard forces destructive vault operations to be authorized by a separate principal in a different scope or tenant.

choices.text: Customer-managed keys for vault encryption with key rotation enforced by Azure Key Vault
choices.explanation: CMK protects backup data confidentiality but does not require approval for destructive operations.

choices.text: Immutable vault, which makes the entire vault read-only after creation
choices.explanation: Immutable vaults prevent certain configuration changes once locked, but they do not implement cross-tenant approval workflow.

choices.text: Private endpoints on the Recovery Services vault to restrict management plane access
choices.explanation: Private endpoints control network exposure, not approval for destructive operations.

questions.tip: Look for the feature that introduces a two-party approval pattern via a separate guard resource.
questions.explanation:
Multi-user authorization through a Resource Guard requires a privileged actor in a separate scope (often a separate tenant) to approve destructive backup operations.

**Why it works:** The vault is associated with a Resource Guard whose Contributor role lives in another scope; destructive actions require explicit authorization from that scope.

**Why the others don't work:**
- CMK: encryption only.
- Immutable vault: limits irreversible setting changes but does not provide approval workflow.
- Private endpoints: network control only.

skills: 1.3.8: Configure security controls for backup protection by using Azure Backup security features
questions.question: Match each Azure Backup security feature to the protection it primarily delivers.

slots.label: Soft delete
Multi-user authorization with Resource Guard
Immutable vault
Cross-region restore

choices.text: Retains deleted backup items in a recoverable state for a defined retention period
choices.explanation: Soft delete recovers from deletion.

choices.text: Requires a privileged principal in a separate scope to approve destructive vault operations
choices.explanation: MUA implements two-party approval.

choices.text: Prevents recovery points from being made less restrictive after the vault is configured
choices.explanation: Immutable vaults lock destructive configuration changes.

choices.text: Allows recovery of backup data from the paired Azure region during a regional outage
choices.explanation: CRR provides regional resilience.

questions.tip: Distinguish deletion recovery, approval enforcement, immutability, and regional resilience.
questions.explanation: Each Azure Backup feature aligns with a distinct protective control: deletion recovery, dual control, immutability, or regional resilience.

skills: 1.3.9: Implement and configure security controls by using infrastructure as code
questions.question:
The platform team commits Bicep templates to a GitHub repository connected to Microsoft Defender for Cloud through Defender CSPM. They want misconfigurations in those templates to be surfaced as comments on pull requests before merge.

Which capability provides this behaviour?

choices.text: Microsoft Security DevOps with pull request annotations enabled in the GitHub connector
choices.explanation: PR annotations from MSDO post inline comments on pull requests for IaC misconfigurations.

choices.text: Azure Policy GuestConfiguration scans applied to the GitHub-hosted runners
choices.explanation: GuestConfiguration scans Azure VMs, not source repositories.

choices.text: Microsoft Defender for Containers running Trivy against the Bicep template
choices.explanation: Defender for Containers scans container images, not raw IaC files.

choices.text: Azure Resource Manager what-if previews triggered by the pull request workflow
choices.explanation: What-if shows resource diffs but does not surface security findings or annotate PRs.

questions.tip: Look for the Defender for Cloud DevOps feature that integrates with source control PRs.
questions.explanation:
Pull request annotations through Microsoft Security DevOps post IaC findings directly as PR comments.

**Why it works:** Defender CSPM connects to GitHub and uses MSDO to scan IaC; PR annotations call out misconfigurations before merge.

**Why the others don't work:**
- GuestConfiguration: VM scope, not repos.
- Defender for Containers: image scanning.
- What-if: deployment preview, no security findings.

skills: 1.3.9: Implement and configure security controls by using infrastructure as code
questions.question:
The security team wants to trace an attack path identified in Microsoft Defender for Cloud back to the specific Terraform file and line that introduced the misconfiguration.

What should they enable?

choices.text: Code-to-cloud mapping in Defender CSPM, with the DevOps environments connected to the repositories
choices.explanation: Code-to-cloud mapping links live cloud resources back to the IaC file and commit that produced them.

choices.text: Continuous export of Secure Score to Log Analytics with a custom KQL query
choices.explanation: Log Analytics export records scores but does not link findings to specific lines of IaC.

choices.text: Activity log diagnostic settings on the subscription that contains the deployed resources
choices.explanation: Activity logs show ARM operations but not the source IaC file.

choices.text: Microsoft Sentinel UEBA enrichment of resource creation events
choices.explanation: UEBA models user behaviour, not IaC provenance.

questions.tip: Identify the Defender CSPM feature that links runtime resources to source artifacts.
questions.explanation:
Code-to-cloud mapping in Defender CSPM connects deployed resources to the IaC files and commits that created them.

**Why it works:** Once DevOps environments are connected, Defender for Cloud surfaces the file, line, and commit responsible for a finding within attack paths.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Log Analytics export: scores only.
- Activity logs: ARM-level, no source context.
- Sentinel UEBA: behaviour analytics.

skills: 1.3.9: Implement and configure security controls by using infrastructure as code
questions.question:
The DevOps team is onboarding their GitHub organization to Microsoft Defender for Cloud so that IaC misconfigurations are flagged on pull requests.

Arrange the configuration steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Enable Defender CSPM on the Azure subscription that will host the DevOps connector
choices.explanation: Defender CSPM provides the DevOps posture features and must be enabled first.

choices.text: Create a GitHub connector in Defender for Cloud and authorise access to the GitHub organization
choices.explanation: The connector links the GitHub organization to the Defender for Cloud environment.

choices.text: Install the Microsoft Security DevOps action in the GitHub repositories that contain the IaC
choices.explanation: MSDO runs the scanning tools that produce the findings.

choices.text: Enable pull request annotations in the DevOps environment settings so findings appear inline on PRs
choices.explanation: PR annotations surface the scan results where developers review code.

questions.tip: Plan-side licensing first, then connector, then scanner, then experience.
questions.explanation: The supported onboarding flow enables the CSPM plan, connects GitHub, installs the MSDO scanner, then turns on PR annotations.

skills: 2.1.1: Implement and configure security for storage accounts
questions.question:
During a security audit, the team finds that several production storage accounts still accept requests authenticated with account keys. Leadership wants all data plane access to flow through Microsoft Entra ID identities, and any legacy SDK call that presents an account key must be rejected at the service.

What should you configure on each storage account?

choices.text: Set the `allowSharedKeyAccess` property to false on the storage account
choices.explanation: This causes the storage service to reject any request that authenticates with an account key, leaving only Entra ID authorization.

choices.text: Remove the Storage Account Key Operator Service Role assignment from every user and group
choices.explanation: That role controls who can list or regenerate keys, not whether shared key requests are accepted.

choices.text: Enable infrastructure encryption on the storage account and rotate `key1` and `key2`
choices.explanation: Infrastructure encryption protects data at rest and does not change the authorization model.

choices.text: Set the minimum TLS version to 1.2 and disable public network access on the storage account
choices.explanation: These settings improve transport and network controls but do not block shared key authorization.

questions.tip: Identify the property that controls the authorization method itself, not who manages keys or how data is encrypted.
questions.explanation:
Setting `allowSharedKeyAccess` to false is the supported way to force Entra ID authorization on a storage account.

**Why it works:** With the property disabled, the storage service returns 403 for any request signed with an account key, regardless of role assignments.

**Why the others don't work:**
- The key operator role governs key management, not request authorization.
- Infrastructure encryption is unrelated to how requests are authorized.
- TLS and network rules do not control the authorization path.

skills: 2.1.1: Implement and configure security for storage accounts
questions.question:
The compliance team requires that a storage account holding regulated documents be encrypted with a key that the organization controls and can rotate independently of Microsoft. The key must be stored in a service that supports soft delete and purge protection.

Which encryption configuration should you apply?

choices.text: Configure customer-managed keys on the storage account using an Azure Key Vault that has soft delete and purge protection enabled
choices.explanation: Customer-managed keys in Key Vault give the organization full control over the key lifecycle and are required to use a vault with purge protection.

choices.text: Enable Microsoft-managed key encryption and request a custom rotation schedule through an Azure support ticket
choices.explanation: Microsoft-managed keys are rotated by the platform and cannot be controlled by the customer.

choices.text: Enable infrastructure encryption with Microsoft-managed keys and store a copy of the key material in Azure Key Vault
choices.explanation: Infrastructure encryption adds a second platform-managed layer but does not give the customer control of the key.

choices.text: Use client-side encryption with the Azure Storage SDK and store the data encryption key as a secret in Azure Key Vault
choices.explanation: Client-side encryption changes the application model and is not the at-rest server-side option the requirement asks for.

questions.tip: Focus on which option lets the customer own the key lifecycle for at-rest encryption.
questions.explanation:
Customer-managed keys on a storage account, backed by Azure Key Vault with soft delete and purge protection, meet the control and rotation requirement.

**Why it works:** The storage account wraps its data encryption keys with a key the customer controls in Key Vault, and the platform requires the vault to have soft delete and purge protection to prevent accidental loss.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Microsoft-managed keys are rotated by Azure on its own schedule.
- Infrastructure encryption is an additional layer using platform keys, not a customer-controlled key.
- Client-side encryption is an application pattern, not server-side customer-managed key encryption.

skills: 2.1.1: Implement and configure security for storage accounts
questions.question:
The legal team needs a blob container that holds financial records to satisfy WORM compliance for a fixed seven-year retention period, with the option to extend retention on individual blobs during active litigation. The configuration must prevent deletion or modification by any identity, including storage account owners.

Which TWO actions should you take?

choices.text: Apply a time-based retention policy of seven years to the container and lock the policy after validation
choices.explanation: A locked time-based policy enforces WORM for the required retention period and cannot be reduced or removed.

choices.text: Apply a legal hold tag to individual blobs that become subject to litigation
choices.explanation: Legal holds extend immutability on specific blobs independently of the time-based policy.

choices.text: Configure a lifecycle management rule to move blobs to the archive tier after seven years and then delete them
choices.explanation: Lifecycle rules do not provide WORM immutability and could be modified by an account owner.

choices.text: Assign a deny lock at the resource group level for the storage account
choices.explanation: Resource locks restrict management plane changes but do not prevent blob modification or deletion on the data plane.

choices.text: Enable soft delete for blobs with a retention period of seven years
choices.explanation: Soft delete recovers deleted blobs within a window but does not block deletion or modification in the first place.

questions.tip: Distinguish features that block writes and deletes on the data plane from features that recover or audit changes.
questions.explanation:
A locked time-based retention policy and per-blob legal holds together provide the WORM and litigation-extension behavior the legal team requires.

**Why it works:** A locked time-based policy guarantees blobs cannot be deleted or overwritten before the retention period expires, and legal holds keep individual blobs immutable for as long as the hold is in place.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Lifecycle rules are management features and do not enforce immutability.
- Resource locks only protect against management plane changes.
- Soft delete recovers deleted data but does not prevent the deletion itself.

skills: 2.1.2: Configure Azure Storage firewall rules
questions.question:
The operations team is locking down a storage account that holds backup files. Only virtual machines in a specific subnet of an existing virtual network should reach the blob endpoint, and all other public traffic must be blocked by default.

What should you configure on the storage account firewall?

choices.text: Set the default action to Deny and add a virtual network rule that allows the specific subnet with the storage service endpoint enabled
choices.explanation: Setting the default action to Deny blocks all other traffic, and a virtual network rule with a service endpoint allows the chosen subnet.

choices.text: Set the default action to Allow and add an IP rule for the public NAT gateway address used by the subnet
choices.explanation: Leaving the default action as Allow keeps the storage account open to all networks.

choices.text: Disable public network access entirely and create a service endpoint policy on the subnet
choices.explanation: Disabling public access blocks the subnet too unless private endpoints are also configured.

choices.text: Set the default action to Deny and add an IP rule for the entire address range of the virtual network
choices.explanation: Storage firewall IP rules do not accept RFC1918 private addresses used inside virtual networks.

questions.tip: Think about which firewall components combine to restrict access to a single subnet.
questions.explanation:
A default-deny posture combined with a virtual network rule for the specific subnet is the supported pattern for restricting a storage account to a single subnet.

**Why it works:** Default Deny blocks all unspecified networks, and the virtual network rule with the storage service endpoint enabled lets the chosen subnet reach the storage account over the Azure backbone.

**Why the others don't work:**
- A default Allow action leaves the account exposed to all networks.
- Disabling public access cuts off the subnet unless a private endpoint is added.
- IP rules cannot use private virtual network address ranges.

skills: 2.1.2: Configure Azure Storage firewall rules
questions.question:
Following a board decision, the storage firewall on a sensitive storage account is set to default deny with only one corporate subnet allowed. Azure Backup now fails to write recovery points because it originates from Microsoft service IPs that are not in any allowed network.

Which configuration should you enable on the storage account?

choices.text: Enable the Allow Azure services on the trusted services list exception on the storage account firewall
choices.explanation: This exception permits trusted Microsoft services such as Azure Backup to access the storage account while the default deny remains in place.

choices.text: Add the published Microsoft service tag ranges as IP rules on the storage account firewall
choices.explanation: Service tag ranges change frequently and storage firewall IP rules do not accept service tags.

choices.text: Change the firewall default action to Allow and add a deny rule for the public internet
choices.explanation: The storage firewall does not support deny rules and reversing the default exposes the account.

choices.text: Grant the Storage Blob Data Contributor role to the Azure Backup service principal on the storage account
choices.explanation: Role assignments authorize identities but do not bypass network firewall rules.

questions.tip: Look for a built-in exception designed for Microsoft platform services rather than network or RBAC fixes.
questions.explanation:
The trusted Microsoft services exception is the supported way to allow services like Azure Backup through a storage firewall that is otherwise deny by default.

**Why it works:** Enabling the trusted services exception grants resource instances of named Microsoft services network access while keeping the default deny in place for everything else.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Service tag ranges are not accepted as IP rules and would drift.
- Storage firewalls have no deny list, and flipping the default opens the account.
- RBAC controls identity authorization, not network reachability.

skills: 2.1.2: Configure Azure Storage firewall rules
questions.question: The engineering team is replacing public access to a storage account with a private endpoint in an existing virtual network. Arrange the configuration steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Create a private endpoint for the storage account targeting the blob sub-resource in the chosen subnet
choices.explanation: The private endpoint must exist before name resolution and firewall changes are applied.

choices.text: Link the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net private DNS zone to the virtual network
choices.explanation: DNS linkage ensures clients resolve the storage hostname to the private IP.

choices.text: Set the storage account public network access to Disabled
choices.explanation: Public access is removed only after private connectivity is verified to work.

choices.text: Validate connectivity from a VM in the virtual network using the storage account hostname
choices.explanation: Validation confirms that traffic now flows over the private endpoint before clients are migrated.

questions.tip: Consider which step must succeed before the next is safe to apply.
questions.explanation:
Creating the private endpoint, then DNS, then disabling public access, and finally validating connectivity is the recommended sequence to avoid an outage.

**Why it works:** The endpoint provides the private IP, DNS resolves the storage hostname to it, disabling public access enforces the new path, and validation proves the configuration before clients are cut over.

skills: 2.1.3: Implement Defender for Storage threat protection configurations
questions.question:
The security team is enabling Microsoft Defender for Storage on a blob container where external partners upload documents. They need every uploaded blob automatically scanned for known malware before downstream services consume it.

What should you enable on the storage account?

choices.text: Enable Microsoft Defender for Storage with the malware scanning on upload feature on the storage account
choices.explanation: Malware scanning on upload triggers an antivirus scan for each new blob written to the account.

choices.text: Enable Microsoft Defender for Storage with activity monitoring only and configure a Logic App to download and scan each new blob
choices.explanation: Activity monitoring does not perform malware scanning, and a custom Logic App is not the Defender on-upload feature.

choices.text: Enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud at the subscription level with the Foundational CSPM plan
choices.explanation: Foundational CSPM does not include malware scanning for storage uploads.

choices.text: Enable Microsoft Defender for Storage with sensitive data threat detection only
choices.explanation: Sensitive data threat detection classifies content but does not scan for malware.

questions.tip: Focus on which Defender for Storage capability specifically inspects newly uploaded blob content.
questions.explanation:
Defender for Storage offers an on-upload malware scanning capability that performs a near-real-time antivirus scan against every new blob.

**Why it works:** When enabled, the storage account triggers a scan on each blob write and surfaces results as a blob index tag and a Defender alert.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Activity monitoring alerts on suspicious access but does not scan content.
- Foundational CSPM is posture management, not workload protection.
- Sensitive data threat detection focuses on data classification and exfiltration risk.

skills: 2.1.3: Implement Defender for Storage threat protection configurations
questions.question:
Management has decided to roll out Microsoft Defender for Storage across every existing and future storage account in the production subscription. The configuration must apply uniformly without per-account enablement.

Which approach should you use?

choices.text: Enable the Microsoft Defender for Storage plan at the subscription level in Defender for Cloud
choices.explanation: Subscription-level enablement applies the plan to all current and future storage accounts in the subscription.

choices.text: Run a script that iterates over each storage account and turns on Defender for Storage per resource
choices.explanation: Per-resource enablement leaves new storage accounts unprotected until the script runs again.

choices.text: Apply an Azure Policy that audits storage accounts without Defender for Storage but does not remediate them
choices.explanation: An audit-only policy reports but does not enable the plan.

choices.text: Enable Defender for Cloud Foundational CSPM at the management group level
choices.explanation: Foundational CSPM does not include the Defender for Storage workload protection plan.

questions.tip: Think about the scope at which Defender for Storage covers both existing and future resources without manual steps.
questions.explanation:
Enabling the Defender for Storage plan at the subscription level is the supported way to protect all storage accounts uniformly.

**Why it works:** Subscription-level enablement registers the plan once and applies it automatically to new storage accounts as they are created.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Per-account scripts miss future accounts between runs.
- Audit policies only report state.
- Foundational CSPM does not provide workload protection.

skills: 2.1.3: Implement Defender for Storage threat protection configurations
questions.question: Match each Microsoft Defender for Storage capability to the security outcome it primarily delivers.

slots.label: Malware scanning on upload
Sensitive data threat detection
Activity monitoring

choices.text: Performs an antivirus scan of newly uploaded blobs and tags or alerts on malicious content
choices.explanation: Maps to malware scanning on upload.

choices.text: Identifies storage accounts holding sensitive data and prioritizes alerts that involve those resources
choices.explanation: Maps to sensitive data threat detection.

choices.text: Generates alerts on anomalous data plane operations such as unusual access patterns or suspicious IPs
choices.explanation: Maps to activity monitoring.

questions.tip: Think about whether each feature inspects content, classifies data, or watches access behavior.
questions.explanation: Each Defender for Storage feature targets a different surface: file content, data sensitivity, and access behavior.

skills: 2.1.4: Manage access to storage, including access policies
questions.question:
The engineering team is building a web application that needs to grant a signed-in user a short-lived URL to download a specific blob. The URL must not be tied to a storage account key and must reflect the user's Entra ID identity in storage logs.

Which type of shared access signature should the application use?

choices.text: Request a user delegation SAS signed with a Microsoft Entra ID credential
choices.explanation: User delegation SAS is signed using Entra ID and ties the signature to the delegated user identity.

choices.text: Generate an account SAS using the primary storage account key
choices.explanation: Account SAS uses an account key and does not reflect the user's identity in storage logs.

choices.text: Issue a service SAS signed by the storage account key with a stored access policy
choices.explanation: Service SAS is also signed with the account key and is not identity bound.

choices.text: Embed the storage account key in the application and let it generate URLs on demand
choices.explanation: Embedding account keys violates the requirement to avoid key-bound credentials.

questions.tip: Identify the SAS variant that is signed using Entra ID rather than an account key.
questions.explanation:
User delegation SAS is the recommended way to issue short-lived URLs that remain bound to an Entra ID identity.

**Why it works:** The SAS is signed with a user delegation key obtained from Entra ID, so the identity is auditable and the signature is not tied to an account key.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Account SAS uses the storage account key.
- Service SAS with a stored access policy is also key based.
- Embedding the key contradicts the requirement to avoid key-bound credentials.

skills: 2.1.4: Manage access to storage, including access policies
questions.question:
To reduce infrastructure costs, a partner integration is issuing long-lived service SAS tokens for a blob container. The security team wants the ability to revoke any issued SAS immediately if a partner is offboarded, without rotating the storage account key.

Which configuration should you use?

choices.text: Associate the service SAS tokens with a stored access policy on the container and delete the policy to revoke
choices.explanation: A stored access policy lets you revoke all SAS tokens that reference it by deleting or modifying the policy.

choices.text: Set a short expiry on each SAS token and ask the partner to refresh frequently
choices.explanation: Short expiry reduces exposure but does not revoke already issued tokens.

choices.text: Rotate both storage account keys whenever a partner is offboarded
choices.explanation: Key rotation revokes every SAS in the account and disrupts all consumers.

choices.text: Issue an account SAS for each partner and remove the partner's Entra ID account when offboarding
choices.explanation: Account SAS is not tied to an Entra ID identity, so removing the account does not revoke it.

questions.tip: Look for the feature designed to provide granular revocation of service SAS without rotating keys.
questions.explanation:
Stored access policies are the supported way to revoke service SAS tokens individually without rotating the storage account key.

**Why it works:** Each service SAS references the named stored access policy, and deleting or modifying the policy immediately invalidates every SAS that references it.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Short expiry does not revoke an active token.
- Key rotation invalidates every SAS issued from that key, not just the offboarded partner.
- Account SAS is not tied to an Entra ID identity.

skills: 2.1.4: Manage access to storage, including access policies
questions.question:
The engineering team is configuring a workload that runs in one tenant and must read blobs from a storage account in a partner tenant. The solution must avoid sharing account keys or SAS, and must let the partner govern access on their side using role assignments.

Which TWO actions should you take?

choices.text: Configure a user-assigned managed identity on the workload and register it as a multi-tenant application in the home tenant
choices.explanation: A managed identity backed by a multi-tenant app registration can be consented into the partner tenant.

choices.text: Have the partner tenant administrator grant the workload identity the Storage Blob Data Reader role on the target storage account
choices.explanation: Role assignment in the partner tenant is what authorizes the cross-tenant identity to read blobs.

choices.text: Generate an account SAS in the partner tenant and store it in Azure Key Vault for the workload to read
choices.explanation: Account SAS uses a key and violates the requirement to avoid SAS and keys.

choices.text: Enable shared key authorization on the partner storage account and exchange the keys via a secure channel
choices.explanation: Sharing keys directly contradicts the stated requirement.

choices.text: Create a guest user in the partner tenant for each developer and grant them Storage Blob Data Reader
choices.explanation: Guest users authorize humans, not a workload identity, and do not satisfy the workload access requirement.

questions.tip: Think about how a managed identity can be made known to and authorized in another tenant.
questions.explanation:
A multi-tenant workload identity combined with a role assignment in the partner tenant satisfies the cross-tenant requirement without sharing keys or SAS.

**Why it works:** The partner tenant recognizes the workload identity through the multi-tenant app, and the Storage Blob Data Reader role assignment grants the specific data plane access required.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Account SAS reintroduces key-based credentials.
- Sharing storage keys contradicts the requirement.
- Guest users grant human access, not workload access.

skills: 2.2.1: Implement platform-level security configurations in Azure SQL
questions.question:
The security team wants to enable Microsoft Entra authentication on a newly deployed Azure SQL Database logical server so that DBAs can sign in with their corporate identities instead of SQL logins. The current global administrator has Owner rights on the subscription but no role has been assigned on the logical server itself.

Who must perform the initial configuration to enable Microsoft Entra authentication on the server?

choices.text: A user who has been assigned as the Microsoft Entra admin for the logical server
choices.explanation: Only the designated Microsoft Entra admin can enable and manage Entra authentication on the server.

choices.text: Any user holding the SQL Server Contributor role on the resource group containing the server
choices.explanation: Resource-level Azure RBAC does not grant the ability to enable Entra authentication on the SQL server.

choices.text: The original `sa` SQL authentication login created with the server
choices.explanation: Azure SQL Database does not expose a `sa` login, and SQL authentication cannot configure Entra integration.

choices.text: A guest user invited from a partner tenant and granted db_owner on the master database
choices.explanation: Guest users with database-scope roles cannot configure server-level Entra admin settings.

questions.tip: Think about which identity is required to bootstrap directory-based logins on the server.
questions.explanation:
Microsoft Entra authentication on an Azure SQL logical server is bootstrapped by the Microsoft Entra admin assigned at the server scope.

**Why it works:** Setting an Entra admin (a user or group) on the server creates the trust path that allows Entra principals to authenticate and to create additional Entra-based users in the databases.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Generic RBAC roles on the resource group do not configure Entra authentication on the SQL server.
- Azure SQL Database does not have an `sa` login.
- Guest users with only database-level rights cannot configure server-level identity settings.

skills: 2.2.1: Implement platform-level security configurations in Azure SQL
questions.question:
During a compliance review, an auditor asks for confirmation that data at rest in a newly created Azure SQL Database is encrypted, and which key is currently protecting the database encryption key. No customer configuration has been performed since the database was created.

Which statement accurately describes the default state?

choices.text: Transparent Data Encryption is enabled by default and the database encryption key is protected by a service-managed key
choices.explanation: TDE is on by default for new Azure SQL databases with a service-managed key protecting the DEK.

choices.text: Transparent Data Encryption is disabled by default and must be enabled with `ALTER DATABASE ... SET ENCRYPTION ON` before audit
choices.explanation: TDE is on by default for new Azure SQL databases; it does not require manual enablement.

choices.text: Transparent Data Encryption is enabled by default but the database encryption key is protected by a customer-managed key stored in Azure Key Vault
choices.explanation: Customer-managed key for TDE requires explicit configuration; the default is a service-managed key.

choices.text: Only the `tempdb` and transaction log are encrypted by default; data file encryption requires Always Encrypted to be configured
choices.explanation: TDE encrypts data files, log files, and backups at rest, and is distinct from Always Encrypted.

questions.tip: Consider what Microsoft enables out of the box versus what requires customer action.
questions.explanation:
Azure SQL Database enables Transparent Data Encryption by default using a service-managed key.

**Why it works:** New databases are created with TDE on, and the database encryption key is wrapped by a Microsoft-managed key unless the customer opts into customer-managed keys in Azure Key Vault.

**Why the others don't work:**
- TDE is not disabled by default and does not require a manual `ALTER DATABASE` command.
- Customer-managed keys are an opt-in configuration, not the default.
- TDE encrypts data files, log files, and backups, and is unrelated to Always Encrypted.

skills: 2.2.1: Implement platform-level security configurations in Azure SQL
questions.question: Match each Azure SQL platform security capability to the protection it provides.

slots.label: Transparent Data Encryption with service-managed key
Always Encrypted with secure enclaves
Private endpoint via Azure Private Link
Server-level firewall rule

choices.text: Protects sensitive column values from administrators while still enabling rich queries such as range and pattern matching inside a trusted execution environment
choices.explanation: Maps to Always Encrypted with secure enclaves, which supports confidential computing for sensitive columns.

choices.text: Allows inbound TCP connections on port 1433 from specified public IP ranges to all databases on the logical server
choices.explanation: Maps to server-level firewall rules, which gate inbound access by source IP at the logical server.

choices.text: Encrypts data files, log files, and backups at rest using a Microsoft-managed key with no customer configuration required
choices.explanation: Maps to TDE with a service-managed key, which is on by default for new databases.

choices.text: Provides a private IP address inside a virtual network so that traffic to the database stays on the Microsoft backbone and avoids the public endpoint
choices.explanation: Maps to a private endpoint, which exposes the logical server through Azure Private Link.

questions.tip: Distinguish between encryption, identity-aware compute, and network isolation features.
questions.explanation:
Azure SQL exposes several independent platform security controls. Encryption at rest is handled by TDE, granular column protection with confidential computing by Always Encrypted with secure enclaves, private network access by private endpoints, and IP-based access by server-level firewall rules.

**Why it works:** Each capability addresses a different layer (data-at-rest, in-use, network, perimeter) so they compose into a defense-in-depth posture.

**Why the others don't work:** Confusing these capabilities, for example expecting firewall rules to provide encryption or TDE to gate network access, leaves gaps in the security model.

skills: 2.2.2: Configure database auditing for Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance
questions.question:
The operations team is enabling auditing for an Azure SQL Database logical server. They want the audit records to flow into a centralized Microsoft Sentinel workspace where security analysts already query other Azure logs with Kusto.

Which destination should they configure?

choices.text: Send audit logs to a Log Analytics workspace that is also connected to Microsoft Sentinel
choices.explanation: Log Analytics is the supported destination for KQL queries and is the data plane behind Sentinel.

choices.text: Send audit logs to a general purpose v2 storage account and configure Sentinel to read the blobs directly
choices.explanation: Storage is a valid audit destination but Sentinel queries data via Log Analytics, not by parsing blobs.

choices.text: Export audit logs to an Azure Cosmos DB container and connect Sentinel through a custom data connector
choices.explanation: Cosmos DB is not a supported destination for Azure SQL auditing.

choices.text: Stream audit logs to an Azure Service Bus topic so that Sentinel can subscribe to events
choices.explanation: Service Bus is not one of the three supported audit destinations.

questions.tip: Match the analyst tooling to the supported audit sink that powers it.
questions.explanation:
Azure SQL auditing supports three destinations: Log Analytics workspace, Event Hubs, and Storage account. To query audit events with KQL or in Microsoft Sentinel, send them to Log Analytics.

**Why it works:** Sentinel is built on Log Analytics, so audit records written there are immediately queryable and can drive analytics rules and workbooks.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Storage receives audit blobs but Sentinel does not read them directly for analyst queries.
- Cosmos DB is not a supported audit destination.
- Service Bus is not a supported audit destination.

skills: 2.2.2: Configure database auditing for Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance
questions.question:
You are responsible for an Azure SQL Database logical server that hosts 40 databases. Compliance requires that every database, including any added in the future, is audited with the same policy and that records are written to a single Storage account.

Where should you configure auditing?

choices.text: Enable auditing at the logical server level so that the policy applies to all current and future databases on the server
choices.explanation: Server-level auditing automatically covers every database, including new ones, with a single policy.

choices.text: Enable auditing on each database individually and rerun the configuration script whenever a database is created
choices.explanation: Database-level policies require ongoing maintenance and miss newly created databases until reconfigured.

choices.text: Configure auditing on the `master` database only, which propagates the policy to the user databases
choices.explanation: The `master` database does not propagate audit policy to user databases.

choices.text: Enable diagnostic settings on the Storage account that receives the logs and set the source to the SQL server
choices.explanation: Diagnostic settings on the storage account do not pull SQL audit data; auditing must be configured on the SQL side.

questions.tip: Look for the scope that automatically inherits to new child resources.
questions.explanation:
Azure SQL auditing can be configured at either server scope or database scope. Server-level auditing applies to all existing and future databases on the logical server.

**Why it works:** A single server-level policy ensures consistent settings and automatic coverage of new databases without manual steps.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Per-database policies do not automatically extend to new databases.
- Auditing on `master` does not propagate to user databases.
- Diagnostic settings on the destination Storage account do not configure SQL auditing.

skills: 2.2.2: Configure database auditing for Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance
questions.question:
Following a board decision to centralize security telemetry, you must configure auditing on an Azure SQL Managed Instance so that audit events are written both to long-term archival storage for seven-year retention and to the existing SIEM that ingests from a streaming pipeline.

Which TWO destinations should you configure for the audit policy?

choices.text: An Azure Storage account with an immutability policy and a seven-year retention rule
choices.explanation: Storage is the appropriate sink for long-term, immutable archival of audit records.

choices.text: An Azure Event Hubs namespace that the SIEM pipeline already consumes
choices.explanation: Event Hubs is the streaming destination for SIEMs that ingest via Kafka-compatible or Event Hubs connectors.

choices.text: An Azure SQL Database elastic pool configured as an audit sink for the managed instance
choices.explanation: Elastic pools are a compute construct, not an audit destination.

choices.text: A Log Analytics workspace exported nightly to the SIEM via scheduled CSV download
choices.explanation: While Log Analytics is a valid destination, exporting CSVs nightly is not a streaming pipeline and adds latency.

choices.text: An Azure Files share mounted to the managed instance subnet for direct write of audit files
choices.explanation: Azure Files is not a supported destination for SQL auditing.

questions.tip: Pair the supported destinations with the use cases of archival and streaming.
questions.explanation:
Azure SQL Managed Instance auditing supports three destinations: Storage account, Log Analytics, and Event Hubs. Storage handles archival while Event Hubs handles streaming to SIEMs.

**Why it works:** Storage with immutability provides compliant long-term retention, and Event Hubs provides the real-time stream that SIEM ingestion pipelines consume.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Elastic pools are not audit destinations.
- Scheduled CSV exports from Log Analytics are not a streaming pipeline.
- Azure Files is not a supported audit destination.

skills: 2.2.3: Configure Defender for Databases protection across Azure database services
questions.question:
The engineering team is migrating an on-premises PostgreSQL workload to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server. Security wants threat detection alerts such as brute force and suspicious connection patterns to surface in Microsoft Defender for Cloud.

Which plan should you enable?

choices.text: Enable the Microsoft Defender for open-source relational databases plan on the subscription
choices.explanation: PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB single and flexible servers are covered by the open-source relational databases plan.

choices.text: Enable the Microsoft Defender for Azure SQL database servers plan on the subscription
choices.explanation: The Azure SQL plan covers Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, not PostgreSQL.

choices.text: Enable the Microsoft Defender for SQL servers on machines plan on the subscription
choices.explanation: This plan covers SQL Server installed on virtual machines or Azure Arc, not Azure Database for PostgreSQL.

choices.text: Enable the Microsoft Defender for Azure Cosmos DB plan on the subscription
choices.explanation: Cosmos DB is a separate Defender plan and does not cover PostgreSQL.

questions.tip: Match the database engine family to the corresponding Defender plan.
questions.explanation:
Microsoft Defender for Databases is composed of multiple plans, one of which protects open-source relational databases including PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB on both single and flexible server deployments.

**Why it works:** Enabling the open-source relational databases plan turns on anomaly detection and brute-force alerts for Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server.

**Why the others don't work:**
- The Azure SQL database servers plan only protects Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance.
- The SQL servers on machines plan covers VM and Arc-based SQL Server installations.
- The Cosmos DB plan protects only Cosmos DB accounts.

skills: 2.2.3: Configure Defender for Databases protection across Azure database services
questions.question:
You are enabling vulnerability assessment for an Azure SQL Database server and want to avoid the operational burden of provisioning and maintaining a dedicated Storage account for scan results. The team accepts the trade-off that classic, customer-controlled storage features are not required.

Which configuration should you use?

choices.text: Use the express configuration for SQL vulnerability assessment, which stores baseline and scan results within the Defender for Cloud service
choices.explanation: The express configuration removes the storage account requirement and is the recommended default.

choices.text: Use the classic configuration and supply a Storage account in the same region as the SQL server
choices.explanation: Classic requires a storage account, which is exactly what the team wants to avoid.

choices.text: Disable vulnerability assessment and rely solely on threat detection alerts to identify misconfigurations
choices.explanation: Threat detection does not perform configuration scans for weak passwords or excessive permissions.

choices.text: Deploy the SQL Server vulnerability assessment extension to the underlying Azure SQL Database compute node
choices.explanation: Azure SQL Database is a PaaS service with no customer access to the compute node for extensions.

questions.tip: Look for the option that removes the storage dependency.
questions.explanation:
SQL vulnerability assessment supports two modes. The express configuration stores results in the Defender for Cloud service and removes the requirement to manage a Storage account.

**Why it works:** Express requires no storage and provides scans for configuration drift, weak passwords, and excessive permissions out of the box.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Classic requires a customer-provided storage account.
- Threat detection does not replace configuration scanning.
- Azure SQL Database is PaaS and does not allow extension deployment to compute nodes.

skills: 2.2.3: Configure Defender for Databases protection across Azure database services
questions.question: Match each database workload to the Microsoft Defender for Databases plan that protects it.

slots.label: Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance
SQL Server 2022 running on an Azure Arc enabled on-premises Windows server
Azure Cosmos DB account using the NoSQL API
Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server

choices.text: Microsoft Defender for Azure SQL database servers
choices.explanation: Covers the Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance PaaS services.

choices.text: Microsoft Defender for Azure Cosmos DB
choices.explanation: Covers Cosmos DB accounts with threat detection for the data plane.

choices.text: Microsoft Defender for SQL servers on machines
choices.explanation: Covers SQL Server installed on Azure virtual machines and Azure Arc enabled machines.

choices.text: Microsoft Defender for open-source relational databases
choices.explanation: Covers PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB single and flexible servers.

questions.tip: Group services by engine family and hosting model before matching.
questions.explanation:
Defender for Databases is split into engine-specific plans so customers can enable only what they run. PaaS Azure SQL, SQL on machines or Arc, Cosmos DB, and open-source relational engines each have their own plan.

**Why it works:** Plan boundaries align to billing and capability so enabling the correct plan delivers tailored detections such as SQL injection for SQL, brute force for open-source engines, and data exfiltration for Cosmos DB.
